PSYCHIATRY__Mental Health Law & Capacity:
Overview — mental health law & capacity
Two distinct legal frameworks (England & Wales). The Mental Capacity Act 2005 (MCA) governs decision-making for people who may lack capacity — any decision, any setting. The Mental Health Act 1983 (amended 2007, MHA) governs the compulsory assessment and treatment of a mental disorder — i.e. detention.
The organising principle: they answer different questions. The MCA asks "can this person make this decision, at this time?" — capacity is presumed, decision- and time-specific, and if absent you act in their best interests, least restrictively. The MHA asks "does this person need compulsory admission/treatment for a mental disorder in the interests of their health, their safety, or the protection of others?"
Mental Capacity Act (2005) Mental Health Act (1983/2007)
Purposemake / support decisions for those who may lack capacitycompulsory assessment & treatment of mental disorder
Applies toanyone ≥16 who may lack capacity for a specific decisionpeople with a mental disorder needing compulsory care
Key test / criteria5 principles + 2-stage capacity test (impairment → unable to understand/retain/weigh/communicate)mental disorder + risk to health/safety/others; requires AMHP + 2 doctors (e.g. s2, s3)
Safeguardsbest interests, LPA, advance decisions, IMCA, DoLS/LPS, Court of ProtectionTribunal, nearest relative, SOAD, IMHA, Code of Practice
The interface (high-yield): treatment for a mental disorder in a detained patient falls under the MHA; the MCA/DoLS covers deprivation of liberty in those who lack capacity but are not detainable under the MHA (e.g. dementia in hospital). Do not use the MCA to give compulsory psychiatric treatment where the MHA is the appropriate route. A patient can be subject to both.
Overview — What & why
Capacity = the ability to make a specific decision at a specific time. In England & Wales it's governed by the Mental Capacity Act 2005 (MCA).
The core concept: capacity is decision-specific and time-specific — a person can have capacity for one decision but not another, and it can fluctuate. You never assess "capacity" in the abstract; you assess capacity for this decision, now.
The framework exists to protect autonomy — a capacitous adult can make an "unwise" decision and refuse even life-saving treatment; the MCA only steps in when capacity is lacking.
The five statutory principles of the MCA
Principle Meaning
1. Presumption of capacityassume a person has capacity unless proven otherwise
2. Support to decidetake all practicable steps to help them decide first (simple language, interpreter, best time of day, communication aids)
3. Unwise decisionsa person is entitled to make an unwise/eccentric decision — that alone does NOT mean they lack capacity
4. Best interestsany act/decision made for someone lacking capacity must be in their best interests
5. Least restrictivechoose the option least restrictive of their rights and freedoms
Two high-yield principles: you presume capacity (the burden is to prove its absence), and an unwise decision is not incapacity (a competent Jehovah's Witness can refuse a transfusion).
The two-stage test of capacity
Stage 1 — the diagnostic test
Is there an impairment of, or disturbance in, the functioning of the mind or brain? (e.g. dementia, delirium, intoxication, brain injury, psychosis, learning disability). It doesn't matter if it's permanent or temporary.
Stage 2 — the functional test: because of that impairment, is the person unable to do ANY ONE of these four? (failing any one = lacks capacity for that decision)
The person must be able to:
1. Understandthe information relevant to the decision
2. Retainthat information (long enough to make the decision)
3. Weigh / usethe information as part of the decision-making process
4. Communicatetheir decision (any means — speech, sign, blinking)
Memory hook: Understand, Retain, Weigh/use, Communicate ("URWC") — failing any single one means no capacity for that decision. Both stages must be met: an impairment (Stage 1) AND an inability (Stage 2) caused by the impairment.
Key features of capacity
  • Decision-specific: capacity to consent to a blood test ≠ capacity to manage finances
  • Time-specific: assessed at the time the decision is needed; can fluctuate (e.g. delirium) → reassess, and delay non-urgent decisions until capacity returns if possible
  • Not based on the outcome: capacity is about the process of deciding, not whether the decision seems sensible
  • Not based on a diagnosis alone: you must show the impairment causes failure of the functional test
Children & young people (a different framework)
  • Under-16s: Gillick competence (a child under 16 can consent if they have sufficient understanding) / Fraser guidelines (specifically for contraceptive advice — cross-ref contraception note)
  • 16–17s: presumed able to consent to treatment, but a refusal can sometimes be overridden by those with parental responsibility/court (differs from adults)
If the person LACKS capacity — best interests
Decisions are made in the person's best interests (Principle 4).
  • Consider the person's past and present wishes, values and beliefs (what they would have wanted)
  • Views of family, carers, and anyone with legal authority
  • Whether capacity might return (delay if possible)
  • The least restrictive option (Principle 5)
Who decides: the decision-maker is whoever proposes the act (often the treating clinician for medical decisions) — not the family (unless they hold legal authority). IMCA (Independent Mental Capacity Advocate) must be instructed for serious decisions (serious medical treatment, change of accommodation) when the person has no family/friends to consult.
Planning ahead — proxies & advance decisions
Mechanism What it does
Lasting Power of Attorney (LPA)a capacitous person appoints an attorney to decide later; two types: health & welfare and property & financial affairs
Advance decision to refuse treatment (ADRT / "living will")a capacitous person can refuse specified future treatment; legally binding if valid and applicable (written, signed, witnessed if refusing life-sustaining treatment)

ADRT point: a valid, applicable advance decision to refuse treatment is binding — even if life-sustaining — but an advance decision cannot demand a specific treatment (only refuse).
Deprivation of Liberty (DoLS / LPS)
  • If caring for someone who lacks capacity involves depriving them of their liberty (continuous supervision + not free to leave), this must be legally authorised to be lawful
  • Deprivation of Liberty Safeguards (DoLS) — the authorisation framework for hospitals/care homes (being replaced by the Liberty Protection Safeguards, LPS)
  • The point: best-interests care doesn't automatically permit detaining someone — that needs separate authorisation

The key discriminator: the MHA can treat a mental disorder even in a patient WITH capacity (if detention criteria met); the MCA only applies when capacity is LACKING, and covers any decision in best interests.
The overlap trap: you cannot use the MCA to give treatment that a valid advance decision refuses, or to detain someone for a mental disorder where the MHA is the correct route.

Overview — What & why
The Mental Health Act (MHA) is the legal framework in England & Wales for the compulsory admission, detention and treatment of people with a mental disorder — when they won't or can't accept care voluntarily and are at risk.
The core concept: the MHA is about detaining and treating a mental disorder against a person's wishes when specific criteria are met — and it can do so even if the person has capacity. Distinct from the Mental Capacity Act (incapacity, any decision, best interests).
Balances patient safety, public safety and civil liberties; detention ("sectioning") is used only when voluntary admission isn't possible/safe.

A person can be detained/treated only if ALL are met:

2. Riska risk to their own or others' health or safety
3. Appropriate treatment availabletreatment must be available — and "treatment" includes nursing and care, not just drugs
The scope rule (high-yield): the MHA only permits treatment of the mental disorder — NOT unrelated physical illness — UNLESS the physical problem is a cause or consequence of the mental disorder (e.g. refeeding in anorexia nervosa, or treating an overdose taken as part of the mental disorder). For unrelated physical illness in someone lacking capacity, use the MCA.

PSYCHIATRY__Self-Harm & Suicide Risk:
Overview — self-harm & suicide risk
Two closely linked but distinct concepts. Self-harm is intentional self-injury or self-poisoning, regardless of intent — it is a behaviour. Suicide risk is a clinical assessment of the likelihood a person will end their life. They overlap because self-harm is the single strongest risk factor for later suicide, but most self-harm is not a suicide attempt — and many who die by suicide have never self-harmed.
The organising principle: every self-harm presentation triggers a suicide-risk assessment, and every risk assessment asks about self-harm. Assess the behaviour (method, intent, circumstances) and the risk (ideation → intent → plan → access to means, plus static & dynamic risk and protective factors) together.
Self-harm Suicidal ideation & risk
What it isa behaviour — self-injury / self-poisoningan assessment of suicide likelihood
Intentoften without suicidal intent (emotional regulation), but may coexistgauged along ideation → intent → plan → means
Assessmethod, lethality, precautions against discovery, current intent, functionrisk & protective factors; recent losses; access to means; hopelessness
Managetreat injury; psychosocial assessment; safety plan; treat underlying causesafety planning, remove means, appropriate admission/escalation, follow-up
Never miss: asking directly about suicide does not increase risk — always ask. Do not discharge on a risk-stratification tool score alone (NICE advises against using tools to predict/triage); base decisions on a full psychosocial assessment. Every act of self-harm warrants this assessment, however minor it appears.
Overview — What & why
Self-harm = intentional self-poisoning or self-injury, irrespective of the apparent motive — a behaviour, not a diagnosis.
The core concept: self-harm exists on a spectrum of intent — from an act with no suicidal intent (a way of coping with unbearable distress) to a suicide attempt — but whatever the intent, self-harm is the single strongest risk factor for future suicide (~30–50× increased risk in the following year). Every episode is taken seriously regardless of apparent lethality.
Epidemiology: very common (esp. adolescents); ~1 in 5 repeat within a year; ~200,000 hospital presentations/year in England (mostly self-poisoning). Strongly associated with depression, borderline PD (EUPD), PTSD, eating disorders and substance misuse.
The key conceptual shift (NICE NG225, 2022) — AWAY from risk stratification
The most important and most examinable point — a major change from older practice. NICE now advises AGAINST:
  • using risk assessment tools/scales to predict future suicide or repeat self-harm
  • using global risk stratification into "low / medium / high" to decide who gets treatment or is discharged
Why: risk is dynamic and these tools don't reliably predict individual outcomes; stratifying can wrongly deny care to "low-risk" people.
Instead: a collaborative, compassionate psychosocial assessment focused on the person's needs and safety — understanding why the self-harm happened and what would help, not assigning a risk category.
Exam framing: if asked "how do you risk-stratify?", the current correct answer is you don't stratify into low/medium/high — you do a needs-based psychosocial assessment and risk formulation.
The psychosocial assessment (the core of management)
Carried out by a mental health professional at the earliest opportunity: do NOT delay it until medical treatment is completed, and do NOT use intoxication (breath/blood alcohol) to delay it.
Purpose (the "why" matters more than a checklist)
  • Build a collaborative therapeutic relationship
  • Develop a shared understanding of why the person self-harmed
  • Identify the person's needs and ensure appropriate care
  • Produce a risk formulation (a narrative understanding of risks + protective factors) — not a stratified score
What it explores
  • Events/context of the act, mental state
  • Current difficulties and strengths, social circumstances, support network, coping resources
  • Mental illness, substance use
  • Modifiable factors that could increase safety
Factors associated with self-harm and suicide (context, not a scoring tool)
These inform understanding and formulation — but are NOT used to stratify or to decide access to care.
Category Suicide risk factors
Demographicmale sex (higher completed suicide), older age; young people (high self-harm rates)
Historyprevious self-harm (the strongest predictor), previous suicide attempt
Mental illnessdepression, bipolar, schizophrenia, EUPD, PTSD, eating disorders
Substancealcohol and drug misuse
Socialunemployment, social isolation, unmarried/divorced/widowed, bereavement, imprisonment
Act-relatedhigh lethality/planning, precautions against discovery, a final act (e.g. leaving a note)
Protective factors: social support, dependent children, help-seeking, engagement with services, hopefulness.
SAD PERSONS-type mnemonics: worth knowing they exist historically — but note they are the very tools NICE now advises against relying on for prediction.
Immediate management (medical + psychiatric in parallel)
  • Treat the physical consequences according to the act (e.g. paracetamol overdose → N-acetylcysteine; opioid overdose → naloxone — cross-ref toxicology; TOXBASE guides specific poisoning management)
  • Ensure immediate safety in the care environment
  • Do the psychosocial assessment early (don't wait for medical clearance or sobriety)
  • Treat with compassion and without judgement — the therapeutic relationship itself affects outcomes and future engagement
Ongoing management (NICE NG225)
Overarching principle: needs-led care, safety planning, treat the underlying condition, safer prescribing — not risk-tool-driven disposal.
Key components
  • Safety plan (co-produced): developed with the person — warning signs/triggers, coping strategies, sources of support, means restriction, emergency contacts
  • Means restriction: reduce access to means (a key, evidence-based preventive measure)
  • Initial aftercare within 48 hours of the psychosocial assessment if ongoing concerns
  • Treat the underlying condition (depression, EUPD, PTSD, substance use) — often the highest-yield intervention
Psychological intervention (specific to self-harm)
  • Adults: a CBT-based intervention tailored to self-harm
  • Children/young people: consider DBT adapted for adolescents (DBT-A), especially with recurrent self-harm + emotional dysregulation
Safer prescribing (high-yield): for people at risk, prescribe medications least dangerous in overdose, in limited quantities; review access to medicines (prescribed, OTC, herbal) that could be taken in overdose. Admission is based on clinical need and safety — not a risk score.
Special considerations
  • Children & young people: safeguarding assessment; involve family/carers appropriately; consider the wider context (bullying, abuse, social media)
  • Borderline PD (EUPD): recurrent self-harm is common — manage per the PD approach (DBT, don't medicate the disorder itself); avoid punitive responses
  • Confidentiality & consent: respect autonomy, but share information where there's a safeguarding or serious safety concern
  • Repeated presentations: treat each episode on its own merits with the same compassion — never assume "attention-seeking"
Exam pearls

Self-harm = intentional self-poisoning/self-injury regardless of intent; the strongest single risk factor for future suicide.

Do NOT use risk-stratification tools or low/medium/high categories to predict risk or decide treatment/discharge → collaborative psychosocial assessment + risk formulation.

Do it early; don't delay for medical treatment or intoxication; focus on needs, understanding why, and safety.
Suicide risk factors (context)
Male, previous self-harm (strongest), mental illness, substance misuse, social isolation, unemployment, unmarried/divorced/widowed, older age.
Management

Safer prescribing

Specific antidotes
Paracetamol → NAC; opioids → naloxone (cross-ref toxicology).
Approach
Treat every presentation with compassion, without judgement, regardless of repetition.
Overview — What & why
Suicidal ideation = thoughts about ending one's life — ranging from passive ("I wish I wasn't here") to active (thoughts of acting), with or without plan or intent.
The core concept: the modern approach (NICE NG225, 2022) has moved away from predicting risk with tools/scores and towards a compassionate, collaborative assessment that understands distress, identifies modifiable factors and co-produces safety — because risk is dynamic and stratification doesn't reliably predict outcomes.
Suicide is a leading cause of death in young–middle-aged adults; men have higher completed-suicide rates, self-harm is commoner in young women. Most people who die by suicide have contacted a health professional in the preceding months — which is why every contact matters.
The key conceptual shift (NICE NG225) — away from risk stratification
The single most examinable point — a major change from older teaching. NICE advises AGAINST:
  • using risk-prediction tools/scales (e.g. older SAD PERSONS-type scores) to predict suicide or repeat self-harm
  • using "low / medium / high" risk stratification to decide who gets treatment or is discharged
Why: these tools don't reliably predict individual outcomes and can wrongly deny care to those labelled "low risk".
Instead: a collaborative, compassionate psychosocial assessment producing a risk formulation — a narrative understanding of the person's risks, protective factors and needs, not a category or score.
Exam framing: the correct answer to "how do you risk-stratify?" is now "you don't stratify into low/medium/high — you undertake a needs-based psychosocial assessment and risk formulation" (cross-ref self-harm note).
Assessing suicidal ideation (the clinical approach)
Asking about suicide does NOT plant the idea — a persistent myth. Asking directly, sensitively, is safe and essential and often brings relief.
Explore the ideation along a continuum, moving gently from general to specific:
Dimension What to explore

Planwhether there is a plan, how formed/detailed
Intenthow strong the wish to act; ambivalence; what has stopped them so far
Preparationany acts made in anticipation, final acts
Protective factorsreasons for living, dependents, future plans, help-seeking
The approach matters more than the checklist: NICE emphasises the "how" — a compassionate, collaborative conversation to understand why the person feels this way — over mechanically ticking risk items. Corroborate with collateral and assess mental state (mood, psychosis, hopelessness, agitation).
Factors associated with suicide (context for formulation — NOT a scoring tool)
These inform understanding, but are explicitly NOT used to stratify risk or ration care.

Protective factors: strong social support, dependent children, religious/cultural beliefs against suicide, help-seeking, engagement with services, hopefulness/future orientation, reasons for living.
Hopelessness (high-yield): one of the most significant psychological markers — often more predictive than depression severity itself. On mnemonics (SAD PERSONS etc.): worth knowing they exist, but these are the very risk-scoring tools NICE now advises against relying on for prediction.
Immediate management (safety-focused)
  • Ensure immediate safety — appropriate level of observation and a safe environment
  • Do the psychosocial assessment early — don't delay for medical treatment or intoxication (cross-ref self-harm note)
  • Treat any acute self-harm/overdose in parallel (e.g. paracetamol → NAC, opioids → naloxone)
  • Compassionate, non-judgemental engagement — the therapeutic relationship itself affects outcomes and future help-seeking
  • Involve mental health services (liaison psychiatry / crisis team) per severity and need
Ongoing management (NICE NG225)
Overarching principle: needs-led care, co-produced safety planning, means restriction, treat the underlying condition — not tool-driven disposal.
Key components
  • Co-produced safety plan: developed with the person — warning signs/triggers, coping strategies, sources of support, means restriction, emergency contacts
  • Means restriction: one of the most effective suicide-prevention measures
  • Initial aftercare within 48 hours of the psychosocial assessment if ongoing concerns
  • Treat the underlying condition (depression, bipolar, psychosis, substance use, EUPD) — often the highest-yield intervention
  • Psychological therapy: CBT-based interventions; DBT for recurrent self-harm with emotional dysregulation (esp. EUPD)
Prescribing & admission: prescribe drugs least dangerous in overdose, in limited quantities; some antidepressants may transiently increase suicidal thoughts in under-25s → closer early review. Admission is based on clinical need and safety (not a risk score); use the Mental Health Act only if criteria met and needed care is refused (cross-ref MHA note).

  • EUPD: chronic suicidal ideation/self-harm is common — respond consistently and compassionately, avoid punitive responses, manage per the PD approach (DBT, don't medicate the disorder itself)
  • Confidentiality: respect autonomy, but information can be shared where there is a serious safety/safeguarding concern
  • After a suicide: support for the bereaved ("postvention") and staff

PSYCHIATRY__Wernicke-Korsakoff Syndrome:
Overview — the Wernicke–Korsakoff spectrum
Two ends of one disease process caused by thiamine (vitamin B1) deficiency — classically in chronic alcohol excess, but also in malnutrition, hyperemesis, prolonged vomiting and bariatric surgery. Wernicke's encephalopathy is the acute, reversible phase; Korsakoff's syndrome is the chronic, often irreversible amnestic aftermath of untreated (or under-treated) Wernicke's.
The organising principle: same deficiency, different stage. Wernicke's = an emergency you can reverse (treat now with parenteral thiamine); Korsakoff's = the permanent memory deficit you were trying to prevent. Think of them as a continuum — recognising and treating Wernicke's early is what stops progression to Korsakoff's.
Wernicke's encephalopathy Korsakoff's syndrome
Onsetacute / subacutechronic (follows untreated Wernicke's)
Hallmarkclassic triad: confusion, ophthalmoplegia / nystagmus, ataxia (often incomplete)profound anterograde ± retrograde amnesia, confabulation, apathy; other cognition relatively spared
Reversibilityreversible with prompt thiamineoften irreversible
ManagementIV/IM thiamine (Pabrinex) urgentlycontinue thiamine; supportive care, rehabilitation, abstinence
Never miss: in any at-risk patient give parenteral thiamine BEFORE any glucose/carbohydrate load — a glucose infusion into a thiamine-deplete patient can precipitate Wernicke's. The full triad appears in only ~10%, so treat empirically on suspicion; Wernicke's is a clinical diagnosis.
Overview — What & why
An acute neurological emergency caused by thiamine (vitamin B1) deficiency, most often in chronic alcohol misuse.
The core concept: it is reversible if treated promptly with thiamine, but untreated it progresses to Korsakoff's syndrome (irreversible amnesia). The whole clinical priority is recognising it early and giving thiamine before the damage becomes permanent.
Epidemiology: mortality up to ~20% untreated; hugely underdiagnosed (only ~15% diagnosed before death) because the full triad is often absent.
The decisive fork — Wernicke's (acute) vs Korsakoff's (chronic)
Two ends of one thiamine-deficiency spectrum (Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome) — the distinction drives urgency:
Wernicke's encephalopathy Korsakoff's syndrome
Natureacute, reversible (a medical emergency)chronic, largely irreversible
Picturethe triad: confusion + ophthalmoplegia + ataxiaamnesia (anterograde + retrograde) + confabulation
Timingpresent now — treatablefollows untreated/undertreated Wernicke's
Prioritygive thiamine NOW to prevent progressionprevention is the only real treatment
The rule (high-yield): Wernicke's = acute + treatable (triad); Korsakoff's = chronic amnesia + confabulation (the irreversible sequel). Treating Wernicke's prevents Korsakoff's.
The classic triad (rarely complete)
Component Detail
Confusionacute confusional state / global encephalopathy
Ophthalmoplegia / oculomotor signsnystagmus (commonest), lateral rectus (CN VI) palsy, conjugate gaze palsy
Ataxiabroad-based gait / cerebellar-type unsteadiness
Critical caveat: the full triad is present in only ~10–16% → do NOT wait for all three. Any one feature in an at-risk patient warrants treatment. Relying on the complete triad is why the diagnosis is missed.
Other features: hypothermia, hypotension, ↓consciousness/coma, peripheral neuropathy.
Why thiamine? The mechanism
Thiamine (B1) is a cofactor for key enzymes in glucose metabolism — most importantly pyruvate dehydrogenase (pyruvate → acetyl-CoA) and α-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase (in the Krebs cycle). Cross-ref the Krebs cycle / metabolism note.
Deficiency → impaired glucose oxidation → energy failure in high-demand brain regions (mammillary bodies, thalamus) → the neurological damage.
The glucose-before-thiamine danger (critical): giving glucose to a thiamine-deficient patient consumes the remaining thiamine (to metabolise the glucose) → can precipitate or worsen Wernicke's. Therefore give thiamine before (or with) glucose in at-risk patients. If hypoglycaemic, treat it — but give thiamine alongside/immediately.
The neuropathology
  • Thiamine deficiency causes damage + petechial haemorrhage to the mammillary bodies and the medial thalamus (+ periaqueductal grey)
  • Memory link (high-yield): the mammillary bodies are part of the Papez circuit (cross-ref the limbic system note) → their damage explains the amnesia of Korsakoff's (Papez circuit = memory consolidation)
  • MRI: mammillary body atrophy/signal change is specific — but imaging must not delay treatment
Causes / at-risk groups (not only alcohol)
Commonest
  • Chronic alcohol misuse — poor intake + impaired absorption/storage/utilisation
  • Malnutrition / starvation, anorexia nervosa
Other at-risk groups
  • Hyperemesis gravidarum, prolonged vomiting
  • Bariatric surgery, malabsorption
  • Refeeding syndrome (cross-ref eating disorders)
  • Dialysis, malignancy, prolonged parenteral nutrition without supplementation
Investigations (clinical diagnosis — don't delay treatment)
  • Clinical diagnosis — treatment must not wait for tests (a response to thiamine can itself be diagnostic)
  • Bloods: FBC, U&E, LFT + GGT (alcohol), glucose, magnesium (hypomagnesaemia impairs thiamine's action — must be corrected or thiamine won't work), consider blood alcohol level; thiamine levels rarely used acutely
  • MRI brain: supportive (mammillary body/thalamic changes) but negative imaging does not exclude it and must not delay thiamine
  • Caine criteria (dietary deficiency, oculomotor signs, cerebellar signs, altered mental state — ≥2 supports the diagnosis)
Management (the emergency)
Overarching principle: immediate parenteral thiamine, before glucose — do not wait for the full triad or imaging.
Acute treatment
  • Immediate IV high-dose thiamine = Pabrinex (parenteral B-vitamins) — typically 2–3 pairs TDS for 3–5 days, then reducing/oral
  • Give thiamine BEFORE or WITH glucose (glucose alone can precipitate/worsen Wernicke's)
  • Parenteral, not oral, acutely — oral thiamine is poorly absorbed in alcohol misusers
  • Correct magnesium (a cofactor — thiamine may fail if hypomagnesaemic)
  • Small anaphylaxis risk with IV Pabrinex → give with resuscitation facilities available
  • Follow with oral thiamine (100 mg TDS then OD) while at risk / if alcohol dependence continues
  • Treat the underlying cause (alcohol withdrawal management, dietetic input, nutritional support)
Prophylaxis (high-yield): all patients undergoing alcohol withdrawal / at risk (malnutrition, refeeding risk) should receive prophylactic thiamine (parenteral in higher-risk, oral in lower-risk).
Korsakoff's syndrome (the sequel)
A chronic amnestic syndrome following untreated/undertreated Wernicke's — caused by the same mammillary body + medial thalamic damage.
  • Anterograde amnesia (can't form new memories — the dominant feature)
  • Retrograde amnesia
  • Confabulation (unconsciously filling memory gaps with fabricated/distorted information)
  • Sensorium + immediate memory preserved (distinguishes it from delirium)
Largely irreversible → prevention (treating Wernicke's) is the only effective strategy; give thiamine + supportive/cognitive care.
Exam pearls

Confusion + ophthalmoplegia (nystagmus/CN VI) + ataxia — but present in only ~10–16%, so treat on ANY one feature in an at-risk patient.

Give thiamine (Pabrinex, IV) BEFORE/WITH glucose — glucose first can precipitate Wernicke's.
Route & cofactor
Parenteral, not oral, acutely; correct magnesium (or thiamine won't work).
Mechanism
Thiamine = cofactor for pyruvate dehydrogenase + α-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase (glucose metabolism — cross-ref Krebs).

Overview — What & why
Korsakoff's syndrome = a chronic amnestic disorder caused by thiamine (vitamin B1) deficiency, characterised by profound memory impairment with confabulation — most often the irreversible sequel of untreated Wernicke's encephalopathy.
The core concept: Korsakoff's is the chronic, largely irreversible "memory" end of the thiamine-deficiency spectrum (Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome) — a selective, dense amnesia in an otherwise relatively intact patient. Because it's irreversible, the whole message is that it is preventable by treating Wernicke's promptly.
Most common in chronic alcohol misuse, but any cause of thiamine deficiency can produce it (cross-ref Wernicke's).

Korsakoff's vs other causes of amnesia
Condition Discriminator
Korsakoff'sdense anterograde + retrograde amnesia + confabulation, with clear consciousness and preserved immediate memory + other cognition (a selective amnesia)
Dementiaglobal cognitive decline (not selective amnesia); progressive
Deliriumclouded consciousness + inattention, fluctuating (Korsakoff's has clear sensorium)

The key point (high-yield): Korsakoff's is a selective amnestic syndrome — memory is devastated but consciousness, attention and other cognitive domains are relatively preserved (distinguishing it from delirium and dementia).
Clinical features
Feature Detail
Anterograde amnesiainability to form/acquire NEW memories — the dominant, most disabling feature
Retrograde amnesialoss of memories from before onset (often a temporal gradient — recent lost more than remote)
Confabulationunconscious filling of memory gaps with fabricated/distorted information — not deliberate lying; the patient believes it
Preservedimmediate memory, consciousness, attention and procedural memory relatively intact
Otherlack of insight, apathy, disorientation to time
Confabulation (hallmark): the patient genuinely believes the fabricated accounts — it's a consequence of the amnesia (gap-filling), not dishonesty. Memory pattern: anterograde dominates, variable retrograde, but immediate recall (digit span) and procedural learning are preserved — the classic "selective" profile.
The neuropathology (why memory specifically)
  • Thiamine deficiency damages the mammillary bodies (of the hypothalamus) and the medial/dorsomedial thalamus — mammillary body atrophy is characteristic
  • Memory link (high-yield): the mammillary bodies are a key node of the Papez circuit (cross-ref limbic system) — the loop essential for memory consolidation (hippocampus → fornix → mammillary bodies → anterior thalamus → cingulate). Damage → inability to consolidate new memories → the anterograde amnesia
  • Mechanism: thiamine is a cofactor for pyruvate dehydrogenase + α-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase (glucose/energy metabolism — cross-ref Krebs) → deficiency → energy failure in these high-demand structures
Causes & investigations
  • Causes (thiamine deficiency): chronic alcohol misuse (commonest); also malnutrition/starvation, anorexia nervosa, hyperemesis gravidarum, bariatric surgery, prolonged vomiting, malabsorption, refeeding
  • Clinical diagnosis — a chronic selective amnestic syndrome with confabulation in a patient at risk of thiamine deficiency, usually after a Wernicke's episode
  • Bloods: LFT/GGT, FBC/MCV, U&E, glucose, magnesium; thiamine levels rarely used
  • MRI: mammillary body atrophy + medial thalamic changes (supportive)
  • Cognitive assessment: impaired delayed recall, preserved immediate/attention — exclude a global dementia
Management (prevention is everything)
Overarching principle: Korsakoff's is largely irreversible → the priority is PREVENTION (treat Wernicke's) + thiamine + supportive care.
  • Prevention (the key message): prompt, adequate parenteral thiamine (Pabrinex) for Wernicke's / at-risk patients prevents Korsakoff's — why Wernicke's is treated so aggressively
  • Established Korsakoff's: thiamine replacement (still given — modest improvement in some; halts progression), abstinence from alcohol + nutritional support
  • Largely irreversible → supportive/rehabilitative care, cognitive support, structured environment, often long-term care/supervision (many can't live independently)
  • Do NOT expect full recovery — unlike Wernicke's (reversible), Korsakoff's deficits usually persist
  • Give thiamine before glucose in any at-risk patient (glucose can precipitate/worsen the deficiency)

Overview — anxiety & stress-related disorders
A group united by pathological anxiety, fear or a stress response that is out of proportion, persistent, and impairs function. They are separated by what drives the anxiety and its time course — free-floating worry, discrete panic, obsessions/compulsions, or an acute reaction to trauma.
The organising principle: pin down the pattern. GAD = generalised, uncontrollable worry across many domains; panic disorder = recurrent unexpected panic attacks + anticipatory fear; OCD = obsessions driving compulsions; acute stress reaction = transient symptoms right after an exceptional stressor. (In DSM-5/ICD-11 these sit in separate chapters — OCD-related and trauma/stress-related — but they cluster naturally for revision. PTSD is covered as its own topic.)

In every case: screen for comorbid depression, substance use and suicide risk, and exclude organic mimics (e.g. hyperthyroidism, arrhythmia, caffeine/stimulants) before settling on a primary anxiety diagnosis.
Overview — What & why
GAD = persistent, excessive, generalised worry about a range of everyday events/activities, present "more days than not", with physical and psychological symptoms of anxiety, causing distress/impairment.
The core concept: GAD is free-floating, pervasive worry not tied to a specific object or situation — this distinguishes it from panic disorder (discrete attacks), phobias (specific triggers) and OCD (obsessions/compulsions). And organic and drug causes of anxiety must be excluded first.
Common; often chronic and relapsing; frequently comorbid with depression (mixed anxiety-depression is very common), other anxiety disorders, and substance misuse.
First fork — primary, or secondary (organic/drug)?
Before diagnosing GAD, exclude conditions that mimic it:
Secondary cause Clues
Hyperthyroidismtremor, weight loss, tachycardia, heat intolerance → check TFTs
Cardiacarrhythmia (e.g. SVT), phaeochromocytoma (episodic ↑BP/sweating)

Other psychiatricdepression, panic disorder, phobias, OCD, PTSD (distinguish the pattern)
The rule (high-yield): always exclude hyperthyroidism, cardiac disease, and drug/caffeine causes before diagnosing primary GAD.

GAD vs panic (high-yield): GAD = constant, pervasive worry, anxious most of the time (can't always identify one worry); panic = short bursts of intense fear, well between episodes.

Duration: worry present more days than not for ≥6 months. GAD-7 is the validated screening/severity questionnaire (higher = more severe). Risk factors: age 35–54, divorced/separated, living alone, lone parent, female sex, family history, childhood adversity, comorbid physical illness.
Panic disorder & the panic-attack physiology
Panic disorder = recurrent unexpected panic attacks + persistent worry about further attacks.
The "fear of fear" cycle: a panic attack → fear of having another → hypervigilance to bodily sensations → triggers another attack → the cycle self-perpetuates.
Hyperventilation → hypocalcaemia physiology (classic high-yield):
  • panic → hyperventilation → blows off CO₂ → ↓arterial CO₂ → respiratory alkalosis (↑pH)
  • alkalosis increases calcium binding to albumin → ↓ionised (free) calcium → functional hypocalcaemia
  • → peri-oral and peripheral tingling/paraesthesia, carpopedal spasm (the classic "tingling hands/around the mouth")
Cross-ref the acid-base + calcium/neuromuscular excitability notes — alkalosis → ↓ionised calcium → tetany.
Management of panic disorder: CBT first-line; SSRI (or imipramine/clomipramine if SSRI fails); do NOT use benzodiazepines (dependence, worse outcomes). Full detail in the dedicated Panic Disorder topic.
Investigations
  • Clinical diagnosis (history + GAD-7)
  • Bloods to exclude mimics: TFT (hyperthyroidism), FBC, glucose; ECG if palpitations/cardiac concern; review medications + caffeine/alcohol/substance use
  • Screen for comorbid depression and suicide risk
Management (NICE CG113 — stepped care)
Overarching principle: stepped care — education/monitoring → low-intensity psychological → high-intensity psychological OR drug → specialist. SSRIs are first-line drugs; benzodiazepines are NOT for GAD.
Step Intervention
Step 1Identification + education + active monitoring (may resolve milder cases)
Step 2Low-intensity psychological — guided self-help (CBT-based), psychoeducational groups
Step 3High-intensity psychological therapy (CBT or applied relaxation) OR drug treatment (patient choice)
Step 4Specialist referral — severe, marked impairment, high risk, or significant comorbidity
Drug treatment (Step 3)
  • 1st-line: an SSRI — sertraline (most cost-effective; off-label for GAD)
  • If ineffective: an alternative SSRI or an SNRI (venlafaxine/duloxetine) — mind withdrawal risk (worst with paroxetine, venlafaxine) and overdose toxicity (venlafaxine)
  • If SSRIs/SNRIs not tolerated: pregabalin (3rd-line; now a controlled drug — dependence/misuse; caution in pregnancy)
  • Do NOT offer a benzodiazepine (except short-term crisis) or an antipsychotic (primary care)
  • Propranolol helps autonomic symptoms (tremor, palpitations) only — doesn't treat the worry; buspirone an option but not first-line
  • Review early (esp. <25/suicide risk); continue effective treatment ≥1 year (high relapse risk)
OCD (brief — sits in the anxiety spectrum)
Obsessions (intrusive unwanted thoughts/images/urges) ± compulsions (repetitive acts to relieve the anxiety), persisting >2 weeks, causing distress/impairment.
  • Management (NICE, by severity): mild → low-intensity CBT including ERP (exposure + response prevention); moderate → SSRI or more intensive CBT (ERP) (clomipramine if SSRI unsuitable/prior good response); severe → SSRI + CBT + specialist referral
  • ERP: expose to the trigger + prevent the compulsion → habituation → extinction of the response
  • SSRI in OCD: often higher doses + longer than in depression; continue ≥12 months if effective
  • OCD ≠ OCPD (OCD = ego-dystonic obsessions/compulsions the person wants rid of; OCPD = ego-syntonic rigid perfectionism — cross-ref personality disorders)
Full detail in the dedicated OCD topic.

Overview — What & why
Panic disorder = recurrent, unexpected panic attacks (discrete episodes of intense fear with physical symptoms) + persistent worry about further attacks or a maladaptive change in behaviour because of them.
The core concept: the defining feature is the discrete, sudden panic attack peaking within minutes — and the disorder is perpetuated by the "fear of fear" cycle (worrying about the next attack drives the next attack). This distinguishes it from GAD's constant background worry.
Common; often with agoraphobia; frequently misinterpreted by patients as a heart attack → repeated presentations to A&E/cardiology.
The decisive fork — attack vs disorder, and primary vs organic
(a) Panic attack vs panic disorder
  • A panic attack is a symptom — a discrete surge of intense anxiety — that can occur in many conditions (GAD, phobias, PTSD, depression, or a real threat)
  • Panic disorder = recurrent unexpected (unprovoked) panic attacks + persistent anticipatory worry — the attacks come "out of the blue"
(b) Primary vs organic — exclude the mimics:
Mimic Clues
Cardiacarrhythmia (SVT), ACS — chest pain, exertional symptoms → ECG
Hyperthyroidismtremor, weight loss, heat intolerance → TFTs
Phaeochromocytomaepisodic ↑BP + headache + sweating
Hypoglycaemiain diabetics; relieved by glucose
Substancestimulants, caffeine, alcohol/benzodiazepine withdrawal
Respiratoryasthma, PE (can coexist/mimic)
The rule: panic disorder is a diagnosis after excluding organic causes (especially cardiac, thyroid, substance) — but avoid over-investigating once the pattern is clear (reinforces health anxiety).
The panic attack (the clinical picture)
A discrete episode of intense fear peaking within ~10 minutes, with ≥4 of:
Autonomic / physical
  • palpitations, tachycardia, sweating, trembling
  • chest pain/tightness, shortness of breath, choking sensation
  • nausea, dizziness, tingling/paraesthesia, chills/hot flushes
Psychological
  • fear of dying
  • fear of losing control / "going mad"
  • derealisation / depersonalisation
Attacks are self-limiting (minutes) but terrifying; patients often believe they're having a heart attack.
The "fear of fear" cycle (the maintaining mechanism)
The central perpetuating cycle: a panic attack → the person becomes frightened of having another → hypervigilant to normal bodily sensations (a slightly fast heartbeat) → catastrophically misinterprets these as a sign of another attack → this triggers anxiety → another attack → the cycle continues.
The point (high-yield): this cognitive cycle of catastrophic misinterpretation of bodily sensations is what CBT targets — breaking the link between the sensation and the catastrophic interpretation. It also leads to avoidance → agoraphobia.
The hyperventilation → hypocalcaemia physiology
The mechanism behind the tingling of a panic attack:
  • panic → hyperventilation → ↓arterial CO₂ → respiratory alkalosis (↑pH)
  • alkalosis → ↑calcium binding to albumin → ↓ionised (free) calcium → functional hypocalcaemia
  • → peri-oral and peripheral paraesthesia (tingling hands/feet/around the mouth) + carpopedal spasm
Cross-ref the acid-base + calcium/neuromuscular-excitability notes — alkalosis → ↓ionised calcium → ↑neuromuscular excitability → tetany. Clinical relevance: explains the tingling, and why slowing the breathing/rebreathing helps (restores CO₂) — though the modern emphasis is on the psychological cause, not just "breathe into a bag".
Agoraphobia (the common association)
  • Agoraphobia = fear/avoidance of situations where escape might be difficult or help unavailable if a panic attack occurred (crowds, public transport, open/enclosed spaces, being far from home)
  • Often develops secondary to panic disorder (avoiding the places where attacks happened) → can become severely disabling (housebound)
  • Panic disorder is classified with or without agoraphobia
Investigations
  • Clinical diagnosis (recurrent unexpected attacks + anticipatory worry)
  • Targeted exclusion: ECG (cardiac), TFTs (thyroid), glucose, consider anaemia bloods; review caffeine/stimulant/substance use
  • Screen for comorbid depression, other anxiety disorders, substance misuse (self-medication with alcohol is common)
  • Avoid excessive investigation once organic causes are reasonably excluded
Management (NICE CG113 — stepped care)
Overarching principle: CBT and SSRIs are the mainstays; benzodiazepines, antipsychotics, and sedating antihistamines should NOT be used.
Step Intervention
Step 1recognition + diagnosis
Step 2treatment in primary care
Step 3review + consider alternative treatment
Step 4review + specialist referral
Step 5specialist (intensive/inpatient) care
The two evidence-based treatments (offer by preference)
  • 1st — CBT (best long-term evidence) — targets the catastrophic misinterpretation cycle; ~7–14 hours
  • 2nd — pharmacological: an SSRI licensed for panic disorder (escitalopram, citalopram, paroxetine) — first-line drug
  • If SSRI unsuitable, or no improvement after a 12-week course → imipramine or clomipramine (TCAs, off-label but effective)
  • Start low, titrate slowly (SSRIs can transiently worsen anxiety on initiation → warn the patient); continue ≥6 months after optimal response
  • Self-help (CBT-based bibliotherapy/computerised CBT), support groups
Do NOT use (NICE): benzodiazepines (worse long-term outcomes + dependence), antipsychotics, or sedating antihistamines for panic disorder.

Panic disorder = recurrent UNEXPECTED panic attacks + persistent anticipatory worry ("fear of fear").

Discrete surge of intense fear peaking within minutes (palpitations, SOB, chest pain, tingling, fear of dying/losing control) — occurs in many conditions.
Exclude organic
Cardiac (ECG), hyperthyroid (TFTs), phaeochromocytoma, hypoglycaemia, substances/withdrawal — but don't over-investigate.

Attack → fear of another → hypervigilance → catastrophic misinterpretation of bodily sensations → another attack (the target of CBT).

Overview — What & why
OCD = a disorder of recurrent obsessions and/or compulsions that are time-consuming (or cause marked distress/functional impairment), persisting >2 weeks.
The core concept: OCD runs on a self-reinforcing obsession → anxiety → compulsion → temporary relief → reinforcement cycle. The compulsion neutralises the anxiety of the obsession, but the relief is temporary and reinforces the behaviour — which is exactly why the treatment (ERP) works by breaking that cycle.
Peak onset 10–20 years; often chronic; frequently comorbid with depression, anxiety, tics/Tourette's and eating disorders; commonly under-disclosed (shame).
The two core components
Component Definition
Obsessionsunwanted, intrusive thoughts, images or urges that repeatedly enter the mind — recognised as the person's own, distressing, and resisted (contamination fears, fear of harm, symmetry, taboo thoughts)
Compulsionsrepetitive behaviours or mental acts the person feels driven to perform in response to an obsession, to reduce anxiety or prevent a feared event (washing, checking, counting, ordering, mental rituals)
OCD requires obsessions and/or compulsions — commonly both (the obsession drives the compulsion).
Ego-dystonic (high-yield): the thoughts/behaviours are experienced as unwanted, irrational and distressing — the person wants to be rid of them. This is central, and the key contrast with OCPD.
The OCD cycle (the mechanism — the target of treatment)
📷 Image placeholder — The OCD cycle — obsession → anxiety → compulsion → temporary relief → reinforcement; ERP breaks it by blocking the compulsion so anxiety habituates
Obsession (intrusive thought → anxiety) → compulsion (ritual) → temporary anxiety relief → reinforcement (the brain "learns" the ritual works) → the obsession returns → the cycle repeats and strengthens.
Therapeutic implication: ERP breaks this cycle — by exposing the person to the trigger and preventing the compulsion, the anxiety is allowed to fall on its own (habituation), so the person learns the feared consequence doesn't happen and the ritual isn't needed.
The decisive fork — OCD vs its key differentials
Condition Discriminator
OCPD (personality disorder)OCPD = ego-syntonic rigid perfectionism the person sees as correct (a lifelong trait, no true obsessions/compulsions); OCD = ego-dystonic intrusive obsessions + compulsions the person finds distressing and resists
Generalised anxietyGAD = realistic worries about real-life concerns; OCD = irrational intrusive obsessions + rituals
Body dysmorphic disorder (BDD)preoccupation with perceived physical defect(s) + related compulsions (mirror-checking) — treated on the same NICE pathway as OCD
PsychosisOCD obsessions recognised as the person's own irrational thoughts (insight retained); psychotic delusions held as true (no insight)
Tics / Tourette'stics are involuntary movements, not driven by an obsession; often comorbid with OCD
The headline distinction: OCD ≠ OCPD — OCD is an ego-dystonic anxiety disorder (distressing, resisted); OCPD is an ego-syntonic personality trait (perfectionism the person endorses).
Risk factors & assessment
  • Risk factors: family history, age (peak 10–20), pregnancy/postnatal, history of abuse/neglect/bullying; association with PANDAS (paediatric OCD/tics after streptococcal infection)
  • Assessment: clinical; ask directly and sensitively (often hidden through shame); assess impact on function and severity (mild/moderate/severe); screen for comorbid depression + suicide risk
  • No diagnostic test; validated tools exist (e.g. Y-BOCS)
Exposure and Response Prevention (ERP) — the key psychological treatment
ERP = the specialised form of CBT for OCD.
  • Exposure: the person is deliberately exposed to the anxiety-provoking trigger (e.g. touching something "dirty")
  • Response prevention: they are stopped from performing the usual compulsion/safety behaviour (e.g. not washing their hands)
  • The result: the anxiety is allowed to rise and then fall on its own (habituation) → the feared consequence doesn't occur → the response is extinguished and the compulsion loses its power
By not performing the ritual, the person learns the anxiety subsides by itself and the feared outcome doesn't happen — breaking the reinforcement cycle.
Management (NICE CG31 — stepped care by severity)
Overarching principle: CBT with ERP is the psychological mainstay; SSRIs (higher dose, longer course) are the drug of choice; combine them in severe disease.
Severity Management
Mildlow-intensity CBT including ERP (guided self-help); if inadequate → SSRI or more intensive CBT (ERP)
Moderateeither an SSRI OR more intensive CBT (including ERP) (>10 therapist hours) — patient choice
Severerefer to secondary care; offer combined SSRI + CBT (including ERP) while waiting
Drug treatment (high-yield)
  • 1st-line = an SSRI (any SSRI; often at higher doses than in depression)
  • OCD needs longer trials — response can take up to ~12 weeks
  • If effective, continue ≥12 months (longer than the 6 months used in depression)
  • 2nd-line: clomipramine (a TCA with strong serotonergic action) — if SSRI ineffective/poorly tolerated or prior good response
Treatment-resistant OCD: after failing an SSRI alone, combined SSRI + CBT/ERP, and clomipramine → refer to a specialist OCD MDT; options include adding an antipsychotic (augmentation) + further intensive CBT.
Children/young people: CBT (including ERP) with family/carer involvement first-line; SSRIs only under CAMHS/child psychiatrist supervision.
Exam pearls
Definition
Obsessions (intrusive unwanted thoughts) ± compulsions (repetitive acts to relieve anxiety), >2 weeks, distressing/impairing; usually both.
Ego-dystonic
Unwanted, resisted, insight retained — the key feature.
The OCD cycle
Obsession → anxiety → compulsion → temporary relief → reinforcement → repeats (ERP breaks it).
OCD ≠ OCPD
OCD = ego-dystonic anxiety disorder (distressing obsessions/compulsions); OCPD = ego-syntonic personality trait (rigid perfectionism the person endorses).
BDD
Treated on the same NICE pathway as OCD.
Risk factors
Family history, peak onset 10–20, pregnancy/postnatal, abuse/bullying; PANDAS (post-streptococcal).
ERP
Exposure to trigger + prevent the compulsion → habituation → extinction.
Management (NICE by severity)
Mild → CBT/ERP; moderate → SSRI or intensive CBT/ERP; severe → SSRI + CBT/ERP + specialist referral.
SSRI
1st-line drug (higher doses, response up to 12 weeks, continue ≥12 months if effective); clomipramine 2nd-line.
Treatment-resistant
Specialist MDT + antipsychotic augmentation.
Overview — What & why
Acute stress reaction / disorder = an intense, transient psychological response to a traumatic event, occurring within the first 4 weeks — with symptoms similar to PTSD but by definition short-lived.
The core concept: it is defined entirely by timing — a trauma response in the first 4 weeks. It sits at the acute end of the trauma-response spectrum: acute stress reaction (<4 weeks) → PTSD (>1 month). Most people recover naturally, which is why watchful waiting, not immediate intensive treatment, is often the right early step.
Common after any significant trauma (accident, assault, disaster, sudden bereavement); a proportion go on to develop PTSD.
The decisive fork — timing (the discriminator)
📷 Image placeholder — Trauma-response timeline — acute stress reaction (<4 weeks) → PTSD (>1 month) → adjustment disorder (non-catastrophic stressor, resolves ~6 months)
The trauma-response conditions are distinguished almost entirely by when and how long — the single most examined point:
Acute stress reaction/disorder PTSD Adjustment disorder
Timingsymptoms within the first 4 weekspersisting >1 month (≥4 weeks)within ~1 month, resolving within ~6 months
Triggersevere trauma (threat to life/integrity)severe traumaany significant life change (divorce, job loss, illness)
Courseusually resolves within days–weekspersistent/chronicresolves as the person adapts
The rule (high-yield): <4 weeks = acute stress reaction; >4 weeks (>1 month) = PTSD. If a trauma response persists beyond a month, the diagnosis becomes PTSD. Adjustment disorder = a maladaptive response to a non-catastrophic stressor.
Terminology: "acute stress reaction" (ICD, the very immediate response, hours–days) and "acute stress disorder" (DSM, the first month) overlap in practice — both denote the early trauma response before the PTSD threshold.
Clinical features (mirror the PTSD clusters, but acute)
Domain Features
Intrusion / re-experiencingnightmares, flashbacks, intrusive distressing memories
Dissociationbeing in a daze, derealisation/depersonalisation, time-slowing, emotional numbing (prominent early)
Negative moodlow mood, distress
Avoidanceavoiding reminders of the trauma
Arousalhypervigilance, exaggerated startle, irritability, sleep disturbance
Distinguishing feature vs PTSD: dissociative symptoms (daze, unreality, time distortion) are often especially prominent in the acute reaction.
Assessment
  • Clinical diagnosis — a clear traumatic precipitant + the symptom clusters + onset within 4 weeks
  • Screen for comorbid depression, substance misuse, and suicide/self-harm risk
  • Exclude an organic cause for altered mental state (head injury, intoxication) if very acute; distinguish from a brief psychotic reaction
  • No diagnostic test; the key is the temporal relationship to trauma
Management (NICE NG116 — psychological, watchful, NOT benzodiazepines)
Overarching principle: most recover naturally → watchful waiting for mild symptoms; trauma-focused therapy if severe; do NOT medicate to "prevent PTSD".
  • Mild symptoms in the first month → watchful waiting / active monitoring, with follow-up within ~1 month (many resolve spontaneously; intensive early intervention can be unhelpful/harmful)
  • Severe symptoms, or acute stress disorder → trauma-focused CBT (TF-CBT) — first-line if intervention is needed within the first month
  • Practical early support: ensure safety, basic needs, social support, psychoeducation about normal trauma reactions
  • Follow up to detect those developing PTSD (symptoms >1 month → reassess and manage as PTSD)
Drug treatment / important correction (high-yield): do NOT offer drug treatment (including benzodiazepines) to prevent PTSD — current NICE. Benzodiazepines are not recommended (dependence, may worsen outcomes). Any short-term symptomatic help (e.g. severe sleep disturbance) should be used very cautiously and is not routine. (Older notes suggesting "benzodiazepines for acute symptoms" reflect outdated practice — same correction as in the PTSD note.)
Exam pearls
Defined by timing
Acute stress reaction/disorder = trauma response in the first 4 weeks; >1 month → PTSD (the diagnosis changes by timing).
Adjustment disorder
Response to a non-catastrophic stressor.
Symptoms
Mirror PTSD (intrusion/flashbacks, avoidance, arousal, negative mood) but dissociation (daze, unreality, time-slowing) is often especially prominent acutely.
Management
Mild → watchful waiting (most recover, follow up ~1 month); severe → trauma-focused CBT.
Avoid drugs
Do NOT use benzodiazepines, and do NOT give drugs to prevent PTSD (current NICE — corrects older teaching).
Follow up
To catch those progressing to PTSD.
Always screen
Comorbid depression, substance misuse, and suicide risk.
PSYCHIATRY__Depressive Disorders:
Overview — the depressive disorders
A group of conditions sharing a core depressive syndrome — persistent low mood, anhedonia and reduced energy for ≥2 weeks, plus cognitive/biological symptoms (disturbed sleep & appetite, poor concentration, guilt, hopelessness). They differ mainly in their context, timing and trigger — not in the core symptoms.
The organising principle: the same underlying depression presenting in a different pattern. Major depression is the baseline diagnosis; seasonal affective disorder is depression with a seasonal (usually winter) pattern; postnatal depression is depression with onset in the perinatal period. Bipolar disorder is covered as its own topic — always screen for a history of mania/hypomania before starting an antidepressant.
Disorder What sets it apart Management nuance
Major depressioncore depressive syndrome, no specific temporal patternmatched care (NG222): antidepressant not routine for less-severe; SSRI + CBT for more-severe; ECT if severe/life-threatening
Seasonal affective disorderrecurrent seasonal onset (autumn/winter, spring remission); often atypical features — hypersomnia, ↑appetite/carb cravingtreat as depression (SSRI/CBT); light therapy is an option
Postnatal depressiononset within ~12 months of birth (peak early weeks); distinct from transient "baby blues"psychological therapy; SSRI (sertraline if breastfeeding); assess mother-infant bond
Never miss: in any depressive presentation — screen for bipolarity (past mania) and assess suicide risk. In the perinatal period also distinguish "baby blues" (self-limiting, <2 weeks) and postpartum psychosis (a psychiatric emergency), and assess risk to the infant.
Overview — What & why
Depression = a mood disorder characterised by persistent low mood, anhedonia and reduced energy, with associated cognitive, biological and functional symptoms, lasting ≥2 weeks.
The core concept: diagnosis rests on three core symptoms + other symptoms + duration, and management is now organised by NICE into a "less severe vs more severe" matched-care model — with the key modern principle that antidepressants are NOT routinely first-line for less severe depression.
Very common; major cause of disability; important overlap with bipolar (always ask about past highs) and high suicide risk (cross-ref suicide/self-harm notes).
The decisive fork — unipolar depression vs the mimics
Before diagnosing primary depression, exclude conditions that present with low mood:
Mimic Discriminator
Bipolar depressionany history of mania/hypomania → changes management entirely (never antidepressant monotherapy) — always ask about past highs
Organic/secondaryhypothyroidism, anaemia, B12 deficiency, Cushing's, medication (steroids, β-blockers), substance misuse
Pseudodementia (older adults)depression mimicking dementia (short history, biological symptoms, patient worried about memory)
Grief/adjustmentproportionate response to a stressor; grief comes in waves with preserved self-worth
Anxiety disordersoften comorbid; distinguish the predominant symptom
The single most important screen: always ask about past manic/hypomanic episodes — missing bipolarity and giving an antidepressant alone risks precipitating mania.
Diagnostic criteria & symptoms
Core symptoms (the key three)
  • Low mood (often worst in the morning — diurnal variation)
  • Anhedonia (loss of interest/pleasure)
  • Reduced energy / fatigue
Other symptoms
  • ↓concentration; guilt + worthlessness
  • Appetite/weight change; sleep disturbance (early morning waking)
  • Suicidal ideation; psychomotor retardation/agitation; ↓libido
Severity (ICD) Criteria (≥2 weeks)
Mild2 core + 2 other
Moderate2 core + 3+ other
Severe3 core + ≥4 other ± psychosis
Biological ("somatic") symptoms (high-yield): early morning waking, diurnal mood variation (worse AM), appetite/weight loss, ↓libido, psychomotor changes → point to more significant depression. PHQ-9 is the validated tool.
The NICE severity reclassification (current)
NICE NG222 (2022) replaced the old grades with two categories, mapped to PHQ-9:
NICE category Includes PHQ-9
Less severesubthreshold + mild< 16
More severemoderate + severe≥ 16
Exam point: know both the classic ICD grades and the current NICE "less severe / more severe" split — they map via PHQ-9 <16 vs ≥16.
Investigations
  • Clinical diagnosis (history + mental state exam + PHQ-9)
  • Bloods to exclude mimics: TFT (hypothyroidism), FBC (anaemia), U&E, B12/folate, calcium, glucose, LFT
  • Assess risk (suicide/self-harm) and screen for bipolarity (past highs)
Management (NICE NG222 — the matched-care model)
📷 Image placeholder — Matched-care flow — PHQ-9 <16 (less severe) → menu of less-intrusive psychological/behavioural options (antidepressant not routine); PHQ-9 ≥16 (more severe) → antidepressant (SSRI) + high-intensity CBT; with review and ≥6-month continuation
Overarching principle: match treatment to severity + preference; antidepressants are NOT routinely first-line for less severe depression.
Less severe depression (PHQ-9 < 16)
  • Do NOT routinely offer an antidepressant first-line — only if it's the person's informed preference (or has worked before)
  • First-line = less intrusive psychological/behavioural options (a menu, matched to preference): guided self-help, group CBT, group behavioural activation, individual CBT/BA, group exercise, mindfulness, IPT, counselling
  • SSRI is on the menu but not preferred over the psychological options
  • Active monitoring if the person declines treatment
More severe depression (PHQ-9 ≥ 16)
  • Offer a combination (matched to preference): antidepressant + individual CBT is typical first-line, or high-intensity psychological therapy, or an antidepressant alone
  • First-line antidepressant = an SSRI
Antidepressant principles:
  • Review at 2 weeks (or 1 week if <25 or suicidal — higher early suicide-thought risk)
  • Continue ≥6 months after remission (reduces relapse; longer if recurrent)
  • Take overdose toxicity into account in those at suicide risk (avoid TCAs)
  • Stop by gradual dose reduction (except fluoxetine) to avoid discontinuation syndrome
Treatment-resistant / severe
  • Switch antidepressant, augment (add another agent), or specialist referral
  • ECT — for severe, life-threatening, or treatment-refractory depression (catatonia, refusing food/fluids, high suicide risk) — see ECT tab
  • Treat comorbid anxiety/substance use; social support
SSRIs (first-line)
Sertraline (adults, 1st-line); fluoxetine (children/adolescents — "fluoxeTEEN").
  • Side effects: GI upset, GI bleeding (give PPI if on NSAID), anxiety/agitation early, hyponatraemia (esp. elderly/diuretics), sexual dysfunction; citalopram → QT prolongation
  • Interactions: warfarin/aspirin (bleeding — avoid co-prescribing), NSAIDs (add PPI), triptans + MAOIs → serotonin syndrome
  • Monitoring: review at 2 weeks (1 week if <25/suicidal); continue 6 months post-remission; reduce gradually in steps over weeks–months, guided by withdrawal symptoms (fluoxetine self-tapers via its long half-life)
  • Discontinuation syndrome (abrupt stop): GI upset, mood change, insomnia, restlessness, sweating, unsteadiness, paraesthesia ("electric shocks")
  • Pregnancy: 1st trimester → congenital heart defects; 3rd trimester → persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn; paroxetine = congenital malformations (avoid); post-MI → sertraline safest
Other classes
Class Key points
SNRIs (venlafaxine, duloxetine)associated with hypertension → check BP before starting + at each titration
Mirtazapine (tetracyclic)blocks α2 receptors → ↑NA/5-HT; fewer interactions (good in elderly/polypharmacy); SEs = sedation + ↑appetite → useful if insomnia/poor appetite ("mirtaZapine — zzz + mmm")
TCAs (amitriptyline, imipramine, clomipramine)not first-line (SE burden + overdose danger); more used in neuropathic pain. Block histamine/muscarinic/adrenergic → "can't see, pee, spit, shit" + postural hypotension + QT prolongation
MAOIs (phenelzine, tranylcypromine)atypical depression (rare); tyramine ("cheese") reaction — aged cheese/cured meats + MAOI → hypertensive crisis
TCA overdose (high-yield): confusion, tachycardia, hypotension, mydriasis, prolonged QRS + QTc, metabolic acidosis, seizures → the most dangerous class in overdose.
Serotonin syndrome (the drug emergency)
Caused by excess serotonergic activity (SSRI + MAOI, SSRI + triptan/tramadol, overdose). Triad: neuromuscular hyperactivity (clonus, hyperreflexia, rigidity, tremor) + autonomic instability (hyperthermia, tachycardia, sweating) + altered mental state (agitation, confusion).
  • Management: stop the serotonergic drug, supportive care, benzodiazepines; cyproheptadine (serotonin antagonist) in severe
  • vs NMS: serotonin syndrome = hyperreflexia/clonus, rapid onset; NMS = "lead-pipe" rigidity + hyporeflexia, slower onset
Electroconvulsive therapy (ECT)
Indications: severe, life-threatening, or treatment-refractory depression — especially catatonia, refusal of food/fluids, strong suicidal intent, or where a rapid response is needed.
  • Only absolute contraindication: raised intracranial pressure
  • Side effects: headache, nausea, short-term memory impairment, retrograde amnesia (events around treatment), cardiac arrhythmia
  • Given under general anaesthesia + muscle relaxant; a course of treatments
Depression variants
Variant Key points
Postnatal (postpartum) depressiondevelops up to 1 year post-birth; low mood, fatigue, poor bonding; distinguish from "baby blues" (within 2 weeks, self-resolving) and postpartum psychosis (emergency); 1st-line = CBT, medication by severity/risk
Seasonal affective disorder (SAD)depression predominantly in winter; treated as depression (psychological therapy → SSRI → light therapy); avoid sleeping tablets
Atypical depressionmood reactivity, ↑sleep, ↑appetite; MAOIs historically used
Exam pearls
Exclude first
Bipolar (ask about past highs), organic causes (TFT), and pseudodementia before diagnosing unipolar depression.
Core triad
Low mood (worse AM) + anhedonia + ↓energy; biological symptoms = early morning waking, diurnal variation, weight loss.
Severity
Mild (2 core + 2 other), moderate (2 core + 3), severe (3 core + ≥4 ± psychosis); NICE: less severe (PHQ <16) vs more severe (PHQ ≥16).
Matched care
Less severe → do NOT routinely give antidepressants → psychological/behavioural menu; more severe → antidepressant + CBT.
First-line antidepressant
SSRI (sertraline adult, fluoxetine child); review 2 weeks (1 week if <25/suicidal); continue 6 months post-remission; taper to stop (except fluoxetine).
SSRI cautions
GI bleed (PPI if NSAID), hyponatraemia, citalopram → QT; avoid with warfarin/aspirin.
Other classes
SNRI (venlafaxine) → check BP; mirtazapine → sedation + appetite; TCA → dangerous in overdose (QRS/QTc, anticholinergic); MAOI → tyramine/cheese hypertensive crisis.
Serotonin syndrome
Clonus + hyperreflexia + autonomic instability + agitation → stop drug, cyproheptadine (vs NMS = rigidity + hyporeflexia).
ECT
Severe/refractory/catatonia; only CI = raised ICP; SE = short-term memory impairment + retrograde amnesia.
Variants
Postnatal depression up to 1 year (vs baby blues <2 weeks); SAD → add light therapy.
Overview — What & why
Seasonal affective disorder = a form of recurrent depression with a seasonal pattern — episodes that reliably occur at a particular time of year (classically winter) and remit at another (spring/summer).
The core concept: SAD is not a separate disease — it is depression with a seasonal pattern specifier. Diagnosis and management are those of depression, with the addition of the seasonal timing and one SAD-specific option (light therapy). Recognise the seasonal recurrence, then treat as depression.
Linked to reduced winter daylight; commoner at higher latitudes and in women; often features "atypical" depressive symptoms.
The decisive fork — is the depression seasonal?
The distinguishing feature is a regular, predictable relationship between mood episodes and the season:
Seasonal affective disorder Non-seasonal depression
Timingepisodes recur at a specific time of year (usually winter onset, spring remission), for ≥2 consecutive yearsepisodes not tied to season
Symptom flavouroften "atypical": ↑sleep, ↑appetite (carbohydrate craving), weight gain, low energyoften "typical": ↓sleep (early waking), ↓appetite, weight loss
Triggerreduced daylight (winter)any/none
The rule (high-yield): SAD = depressive episodes with a consistent seasonal pattern (≥2 years). The winter pattern is classic (a rarer summer pattern exists). A single winter of low mood isn't enough — you need the recurrent seasonal relationship.
Clinical features
  • Core depressive symptoms (as per depression): low mood, anhedonia, reduced energy — but occurring seasonally
The "atypical" features that characterise winter SAD (high-yield)
  • Hypersomnia (sleeping more, not early-morning waking)
  • Hyperphagia with carbohydrate craving → weight gain
  • Fatigue / leaden heaviness, low energy
  • (Contrast with the classic biological symptoms of typical depression — insomnia, weight loss)
Winter onset (autumn/winter), remitting in spring/summer.
Pathophysiology (why light matters)
Thought to relate to reduced winter daylight affecting circadian rhythm and melatonin/serotonin regulation (↓light → altered melatonin secretion and circadian phase) — the rationale for light therapy.
Assessment
  • Clinical diagnosis — a history of recurrent depressive episodes with a seasonal pattern (seasonality history over ≥2 years); PHQ-9 for severity
  • Exclude organic mimics — especially hypothyroidism (also causes fatigue/low mood/weight gain in winter) — and other causes as for depression
  • Screen for suicide risk and comorbidity as in any depression
Management (treat as depression + light therapy)
Overarching principle: treat as depression (per NICE NG222) — psychological therapy and/or an SSRI — with light therapy as a SAD-specific adjunct.
  • Treat as depression (cross-ref): less severe → psychological/behavioural interventions (CBT) first-line; more severe → SSRI + psychological therapy (SSRI = first-line drug)
  • Light therapy (bright light therapy) — a SAD-specific option: exposure to a bright light box, particularly in the morning; can help winter SAD (evidence modest/mixed, so an adjunct/option, but the intervention uniquely associated with SAD)
  • The sequence (from your notes): psychological therapy → SSRI → light therapy
  • Lifestyle: maximise natural daylight exposure, exercise, regular routine
  • Prophylaxis: those with a reliable seasonal pattern may start treatment (light therapy or an antidepressant) before the season begins
Avoid sleeping tablets (high-yield): do NOT give hypnotics/sedatives — the hypersomnia and low energy of SAD are worsened by sedatives (they don't treat the disorder and add fatigue).
Exam pearls
Definition
SAD = recurrent depression with a seasonal pattern (usually winter onset, spring remission, ≥2 years) — a specifier, not a separate disease.
Atypical features
Hypersomnia, hyperphagia + carbohydrate craving → weight gain, fatigue (contrast: typical depression = insomnia/early waking + weight loss).
Mechanism
Linked to reduced winter daylight (circadian/melatonin) → rationale for light therapy.
Exclude
Hypothyroidism (mimics winter fatigue/low mood/weight gain).
Management
Treat as depression (psychological therapy ± SSRI) + light therapy; sequence: psychological therapy → SSRI → light therapy.
Avoid
Do NOT give sleeping tablets (worsen the hypersomnia/fatigue).
Prophylaxis
Consider starting treatment before the season in those with a predictable pattern.
Overview — What & why
Postnatal (postpartum) depression = a depressive episode arising in the postnatal period — meeting the criteria for depression, in the context of new motherhood, and distinct from the transient "baby blues".
The core concept: PND sits in the middle of the perinatal mood triad — baby blues (mild, transient) → postnatal depression (a true depressive illness) → postpartum psychosis (a psychiatric emergency). The key skill is distinguishing the three by timing and severity, because their urgency and management differ enormously.
Perinatal mental illness is common (~10–20% of women) and is a leading cause of maternal death (suicide) in the year after birth — actively screen for it and take it seriously.
The decisive fork — the perinatal mood triad
📷 Image placeholder — Postpartum timeline — baby blues (days 3–10, self-limiting) vs postnatal depression (weeks–months, treat) vs postpartum psychosis (first ~2 weeks, emergency)
Baby blues Postnatal depression Postpartum psychosis
Onsetdays 3–10weeks–months, up to 1 yearacute, ~days 1–2 to 2 weeks
Severitymild, transientmoderate–severe depressive illnesspsychiatric EMERGENCY
Featurestearfulness, mood lability, irritability, anxietypersistent low mood, anhedonia, fatigue, guilt, poor bonding, sleep/appetite changepsychosis — delusions, hallucinations, mania/confusion
