The key discriminator: baby blues resolves on its own within ~2 weeks — if low mood persists beyond 2 weeks or is severe, think PND, not blues. Acute psychosis/mania in the first 2 weeks → postpartum psychosis (emergency).
Clinical features of PND
  • Core depressive symptoms: persistent low mood, anhedonia, fatigue, disturbed sleep, poor appetite, guilt, poor concentration
Perinatal-specific features (high-yield)
  • Concerns about maternal-infant bonding / difficulty bonding with the baby
  • Guilt about not coping / not being a "good mother"
  • Anxiety about the baby's health
Assess (critically): thoughts of self-harm/suicide AND any thoughts of harming the infant — both must be asked about directly.
Risk factors
Past history of depression/PND or other mental illness; family history; lack of social support; relationship difficulties; unplanned/complicated pregnancy or birth; socioeconomic stress; history of postpartum psychosis or bipolar (a major risk for postpartum psychosis specifically).
Screening & assessment
  • Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale (EPDS) — the validated 10-item screening tool (a score ~≥10–13 suggests further assessment; one item screens for self-harm)
  • Whooley questions (the two-question depression screen) are also used
  • Clinical diagnosis (depressive episode + postnatal context); assess severity, bonding, social support, and risk to mother and infant
  • Exclude hypothyroidism (postpartum thyroiditis is common and mimics PND — check TFTs), anaemia, organic causes
  • Distinguish from baby blues (timing/severity) and postpartum psychosis (psychosis/mania — emergency)
Management (NICE CG192 — treat as depression, with perinatal-specific care)
Overarching principle: treat as depression matched to severity, with a low threshold for support; choose medication compatible with breastfeeding; involve the perinatal/health-visiting team. 1st-line = CBT; add pharmacological treatment by severity/risk.
  • Mild–moderate PND: psychological therapy first-line — CBT or IPT, guided self-help; health visitor + social support; often primary care
  • Moderate–severe PND: psychological therapy + an antidepressant
  • Support the mother-infant relationship (bonding-focused interventions); involve partner/family; health visitor + perinatal mental health team
  • Severe/risk to mother or baby: specialist perinatal mental health services; consider admission to a Mother & Baby Unit (keeps mother + baby together)
Antidepressant choice in breastfeeding (high-yield): SSRIs are generally compatible — sertraline (and paroxetine) favoured (low levels in breast milk). Do not withhold effective treatment for fear of breastfeeding — untreated PND harms both mother and baby. And do NOT stop psychiatric medication abruptly in pregnancy/postpartum (high relapse risk) — decide with specialist input.
The other two (brief — for the triad)
  • Baby blues: transient tearfulness/lability days 3–10, resolves spontaneously in ~2 weeks → reassurance and support only (no treatment)
  • Postpartum psychosis (emergency): acute onset (usually first 2 weeks) of psychosis, mania, confusion, or severe depression with psychotic features; strongly associated with bipolar / previous postpartum psychosis; a psychiatric emergency → urgent assessment + admission (Mother & Baby Unit); risk to mother and baby; treated with antipsychotics/mood stabilisers ± ECT
Exam pearls
Baby blues
Days 3–10, mild, resolves ~2 weeks → reassurance only.
Postnatal depression
Weeks–months (up to 1 year), a true depressive episode → treat.
Postpartum psychosis
Acute (first ~2 weeks), psychosis/mania → EMERGENCY, admit; linked to bipolar / previous postpartum psychosis.
PND features
Depressive symptoms + poor bonding/guilt; always ask about self-harm AND thoughts of harming the infant.
Screening
Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale (EPDS).
Exclude
Hypothyroidism (postpartum thyroiditis mimics PND — check TFTs).
Management
CBT/IPT first-line; add antidepressant for moderate–severe — sertraline favoured (breastfeeding-compatible); don't withhold treatment for breastfeeding.
Prescribing
Do NOT stop psychiatric medication abruptly in pregnancy/postpartum (relapse risk).
Severe/risk
Perinatal mental health team + Mother & Baby Unit.
PSYCHIATRY__Transient Global Amnesia:
Overview — What & why
Transient global amnesia = a sudden, temporary episode of profound memory loss — predominantly anterograde amnesia (inability to form new memories) — with other cognitive functions preserved, resolving completely within 24 hours.
The core concept: TGA is defined by its transience and selectivity — a dramatic but isolated amnesia in an otherwise alert, oriented-to-self, fully-functioning person, that resolves fully. The clinical priority is to distinguish it from dangerous mimics (stroke/TIA, seizure) — TGA itself is benign.
Typically affects middle-aged/older adults (50–70); usually a one-off event with an excellent prognosis and low recurrence.
The decisive fork — TGA vs its dangerous mimics
TGA TIA / stroke Transient epileptic amnesia Dissociative amnesia
Memoryanterograde ± some retrograde, isolatedamnesia + focal neurologybrief, recurrent, epileptic featuresoften loss of personal identity
Other neurologyNONE (no weakness/aphasia/focal signs)focal deficitsautomatisms, other seizure featuresnone
Durationup to 24h, full recoveryvariable; may not fully recoverbrief (mins), often on waking, recurrentvariable
Consciousness/identityalert, knows who they aremay varymay have altered awarenessidentity affected
Recurrenceusually one-offmay recurrecurrent (the clue)variable
The rules (high-yield): TGA = isolated amnesia + NO focal signs + full recovery <24h; focal neurology → stroke/TIA (urgent); recurrent brief episodes → transient epileptic amnesia (EEG); loss of personal identity ("who am I?") → dissociative amnesia (TGA patients know who they are).
Clinical features
  • Sudden onset anterograde amnesia — cannot form new memories → the classic repetitive questioning ("Where am I? What are we doing?") despite being answered
  • Some retrograde amnesia (recent memories) — variable
  • Preserved (high-yield): personal identity (knows who they are), alertness/consciousness, attention, language, and complex/learned tasks (can still drive, cook) — the amnesia is selective
  • No focal neurological deficit (no weakness, sensory loss, aphasia, visual field defect) — a defining feature
  • Duration: resolves completely within 24 hours (usually 4–8h); the person is left with a permanent gap for the episode itself
Triggers & associations
Often precipitated by a specific trigger shortly before onset: sudden immersion in cold/hot water, physical exertion, emotional stress, Valsalva-type activities (straining, sexual intercourse), sudden temperature change.
Middle-aged/older adults; the precise cause is uncertain (venous congestion, transient hippocampal dysfunction, and migraine mechanisms have all been proposed).
Investigations (mainly to exclude mimics)
  • Clinical diagnosis (the characteristic syndrome + preserved other functions + resolution)
  • Neurological examination — must show no focal signs
  • Bloods: glucose (exclude hypoglycaemia), U&E, FBC
  • Brain imaging (CT/MRI) if atypical features/focal signs → exclude stroke; MRI (DWI) may occasionally show a small hippocampal lesion in TGA
  • ECG (cardiac source); consider EEG if recurrent/seizure features
Diagnostic criteria (Hodges & Warlow): witnessed attack, anterograde amnesia, no clouding of consciousness or loss of personal identity, no focal neurological/epileptic features, resolution within 24 hours, no recent head injury/active epilepsy.
Management (reassurance — it's benign)
Overarching principle: exclude the mimics, then reassure — TGA is self-limiting with an excellent prognosis and no specific treatment.
  • No specific treatment — the episode resolves spontaneously
  • Reassurance + explanation — benign, self-limiting, low recurrence risk, excellent prognosis
  • Exclude and address any mimic (stroke/TIA pathway if focal signs; EEG/epilepsy pathway if recurrent)
  • Manage vascular risk factors generally, though TGA is not itself a strong stroke risk marker
  • Recurrence uncommon; frequent recurrence should prompt reconsidering the diagnosis (esp. transient epileptic amnesia)
Exam pearls
Definition
Sudden, isolated, temporary amnesia (mainly anterograde) resolving fully within 24 hours, with other cognition + personal identity + consciousness preserved and NO focal neurology.
Classic picture
Repetitive questioning ("where am I?") despite answers; can still do complex learned tasks.
Key task = exclude mimics
Focal signs → stroke/TIA; recurrent brief episodes → transient epileptic amnesia (EEG); loss of identity → dissociative amnesia.
Triggers
Cold/hot water immersion, physical exertion, emotional stress, Valsalva/sexual activity.
Demographics
Middle-aged/older adults; usually a one-off.
Preserved identity
Knows who they are — distinguishes from dissociative amnesia.
Management
Exclude mimics (exam, glucose, ± imaging/EEG) → reassurance; no specific treatment; excellent prognosis.
vs Korsakoff's
TGA = transient + full recovery; Korsakoff's = chronic + irreversible + confabulation.
PSYCHIATRY__Sleep Paralysis:
Overview — What & why
Sleep paralysis = a transient, temporary inability to move or speak at the transition between sleep and wakefulness — on waking (hypnopompic) or, less often, on falling asleep (hypnagogic).
The core concept: it is the normal muscle paralysis (atonia) of REM sleep persisting briefly into wakefulness — the mind wakes before the body's REM atonia has switched off. This is why it's benign and self-limiting, and understood as a REM-sleep phenomenon, not a neurological catastrophe.
Very common (a large proportion of people experience it at least once); usually isolated and benign, but can be recurrent and distressing.
The decisive fork — isolated/benign vs part of narcolepsy
Isolated sleep paralysis Sleep paralysis in narcolepsy
Contextoccurs alone, often with poor sleep/sleep deprivationone of the narcolepsy tetrad
Associated featuresnoneexcessive daytime sleepiness, cataplexy, hypnagogic hallucinations
Significancebenign; reassurancepoints to narcolepsy → needs sleep studies (MSLT)
The rule (high-yield): isolated sleep paralysis is benign → reassurance; but if it occurs with excessive daytime sleepiness + cataplexy + hypnagogic hallucinations, think narcolepsy (sleep paralysis is one of its four cardinal features — cross-ref sleep disorders).
The mechanism
  • During REM sleep, the body is normally in muscle atonia (skeletal muscles paralysed) — this prevents us from acting out our dreams (cross-ref neurophysiology)
  • In sleep paralysis, this REM atonia persists briefly into wakefulness — the person becomes consciously aware but the muscles are still paralysed
  • Duration: seconds to a couple of minutes; resolves spontaneously (or when touched/spoken to)
The link (high-yield): it's the mirror image of REM sleep behaviour disorder (RBD) — in RBD the atonia is lost (dreams acted out); in sleep paralysis the atonia persists into wakefulness. Both are disorders of REM-atonia timing.
Clinical features
  • Transient paralysis of skeletal muscles on waking or falling asleep — conscious but unable to move or speak (breathing and eye movements preserved)
  • Hallucinations (high-yield): often vivid, frightening hypnagogic/hypnopompic hallucinations — classically a sense of a threatening presence, pressure on the chest, or a figure ("Old Hag" phenomenon) → can be terrifying
  • Intact awareness: the person is awake and aware throughout (distinguishing from a seizure or faint)
  • Self-limiting: resolves within seconds–minutes
Triggers & associations
  • Sleep deprivation and irregular sleep schedules (commonest — shift work, jet lag)
  • Sleeping supine (on the back)
  • Stress/anxiety
  • Narcolepsy (as above); other sleep disorders; rarely substance/medication effects
  • Recognised across many cultures (with varied cultural explanations)
Assessment
  • Clinical diagnosis — a characteristic history of transient paralysis at sleep-wake transitions with intact awareness
  • Key task: screen for narcolepsy (excessive daytime sleepiness, cataplexy, hypnagogic hallucinations) → if present, refer for sleep studies / MSLT
  • Exclude/distinguish: seizures, syncope, cataplexy (occurs awake, emotion-triggered), TIA, panic attacks
  • Review sleep hygiene, sleep deprivation and triggers
Management (reassurance + sleep hygiene)
Overarching principle: reassurance and sleep hygiene for isolated cases; treat any underlying narcolepsy; medication only for frequent/distressing episodes.
  • Reassurance + education — explain it's a benign REM phenomenon; this alone helps considerably
  • Sleep hygiene (first-line practical measure): adequate, regular sleep; avoid sleep deprivation; avoid sleeping supine; reduce stress; limit stimulants/alcohol before bed
  • Medication (only if troublesome/frequent): clonazepam (or a REM-suppressing antidepressant, e.g. an SSRI/TCA) can reduce frequency
  • If narcolepsy is present: manage the narcolepsy (cross-ref sleep disorders)
Exam pearls
Definition
Transient inability to move/speak at the sleep-wake transition (hypnopompic on waking / hypnagogic on falling asleep), with intact awareness.
Mechanism
Normal REM muscle atonia persisting into wakefulness (mind awake, muscles still paralysed) — the mirror image of REM sleep behaviour disorder (atonia lost).
Hallucinations
Often frightening hypnagogic/hypnopompic hallucinations (sense of a presence, chest pressure).
Benign when isolated
Self-limiting → reassurance + sleep hygiene.
Screen for narcolepsy
Sleep paralysis + excessive daytime sleepiness + cataplexy + hypnagogic hallucinations = the narcolepsy tetrad → refer for sleep studies.
Triggers
Sleep deprivation, irregular sleep, supine position, stress.
Management
Reassurance + sleep hygiene; clonazepam (or REM-suppressing antidepressant) only if frequent/troublesome.
PSYCHIATRY__Learning Disability:
Overview — What & why
Learning disability (LD) = a lifelong condition comprising (1) significantly reduced intellectual ability, (2) reduced ability to cope independently (adaptive/social functioning), which (3) started before adulthood and has a lasting effect on development.
The core concept: LD is defined by THREE elements together — impaired intelligence + impaired adaptive functioning + onset in childhood. A low IQ alone is not enough. The clinical priority is that people with LD have major, largely avoidable health inequalities — so the whole approach centres on reasonable adjustments, avoiding diagnostic overshadowing, and appropriate (not over-) medication.
Terminology (high-yield): "learning disability" is the UK term (≈ "intellectual disability" internationally). It is distinct from "learning difficulty" (e.g. dyslexia — a specific difficulty without global intellectual impairment).
The three defining criteria (the diagnostic triad)
Criterion Detail
1. Impaired intelligencesignificantly below-average intellectual functioning (IQ < 70)
2. Impaired adaptive/social functioningreduced ability to cope independently — self-care, communication, social skills, daily living
3. Onset before adulthoodpresent from the developmental period (before age 18) — it is lifelong, not acquired in adult life
The rule (high-yield): all three are required — IQ < 70 alone is NOT a learning disability without the adaptive impairment and childhood onset. An adult who loses cognitive function later (dementia, brain injury) does not have a learning disability.
Severity classification (by IQ + support needs)
Severity Approx IQ Functional level
Mild50–69often independent living with support; may have jobs/relationships; the majority
Moderate35–49need support with daily living; some language/self-care
Severe20–34significant support needs; limited communication
Profound< 20full support for all needs; often multiple physical disabilities
Most people with LD have mild LD and can live relatively independently with support; severity guides the level of support, not the person's worth or rights.
Causes
  • Genetic/chromosomal: Down's syndrome (trisomy 21), Fragile X (commonest inherited cause), Prader-Willi, Williams, Klinefelter, Turner's (cross-ref paediatric genetic syndromes)
  • Metabolic: phenylketonuria (PKU) and other inborn errors (newborn blood spot)
  • Antenatal: congenital infection (TORCH), fetal alcohol syndrome, teratogens
  • Perinatal: birth asphyxia (HIE), prematurity, kernicterus
  • Postnatal: meningitis/encephalitis, head injury, non-accidental injury
  • Often no identifiable cause
Associated conditions & comorbidities (LD rarely comes alone)
Much higher rates of:
  • Epilepsy (especially in severe LD)
  • Physical disability, sensory impairment (vision/hearing), cerebral palsy
  • Mental illness — depression, anxiety, psychosis
  • Autism spectrum disorder and ADHD (frequent overlap)
  • Behaviour that challenges — often a communication of distress, pain or unmet need
Key clinical principle (high-yield): behaviour that challenges is often the expression of an underlying problem (pain, constipation, infection, dental problems, sensory overload, distress) → look for the cause, don't just sedate.
Health inequalities & the core clinical principles (the heart of the topic)
People with LD die younger and have more avoidable deaths than the general population — driven by systemic failures, not the LD itself.
Concept Meaning
Diagnostic overshadowingattributing symptoms to the person's LD rather than investigating a genuine physical/mental illness (e.g. assuming distress "is just their LD" when they have appendicitis) — a major cause of avoidable harm
Reasonable adjustments (Equality Act 2010)a legal duty to adapt care — longer appointments, easy-read information, quiet environment, hospital passport
Hospital passporta document the person brings describing their needs, communication, likes/dislikes, how they show pain
Annual health checkpeople with LD (aged 14+) are entitled to an annual GP health check to detect unmet/undiagnosed needs
STOMP / STAMPStopping Over-Medication of People with a learning disability, autism or both (with psychotropics)
LeDeRLearning from Lives and Deaths Reviews — reviews all deaths of people with LD to reduce avoidable mortality
Oliver McGowan Mandatory Trainingstatutory LD/autism training for health & social care staff (named after a young man who died from an antipsychotic given despite known adverse reactions)
The two highest-yield concepts: diagnostic overshadowing (don't blame new symptoms on the LD — investigate) and reasonable adjustments (a legal duty).
Assessment & communication
  • Diagnosis: developmental history, cognitive/IQ assessment, adaptive functioning assessment, identify cause where possible (genetic/metabolic screen), screen for comorbidities (epilepsy, sensory, mental illness, autism)
  • Communication (high-yield): adapt to the person's level — easy-read materials, pictures, short sentences, extra time, involve carers who know them; ASK–LISTEN–DO
  • Capacity (cross-ref MCA note): LD does NOT automatically mean lacking capacity — presume capacity, assess decision-specifically, provide support to decide; best interests only where capacity is genuinely lacking
  • Physical health: proactively screen (they under-report symptoms) — the annual health check exists for this reason
Management (support-based, not "curative")
Overarching principle: a multidisciplinary, person-centred support model — treat comorbidities, make reasonable adjustments, avoid over-medication, and address the cause of behaviour that challenges.
  • Multidisciplinary support: community LD team (LD nurses, psychiatry, psychology, SALT, OT, physiotherapy, social care), education/employment support, family/carer support
Behaviour that challenges (high-yield)
  • First — look for and treat the underlying cause (pain, constipation, infection, dental, distress, environment)
  • Positive Behaviour Support (PBS) — the evidence-based approach (first-line)
  • Avoid psychotropics for behaviour unless there's a clear indication (a treatable mental illness), in line with STOMP — antipsychotics are not a substitute for addressing needs
  • Treat comorbid mental illness on its merits (adjust communication; watch for diagnostic overshadowing)
  • Reasonable adjustments in every healthcare contact; hospital passport; annual health check
  • Safeguarding: people with LD are at higher risk of abuse/neglect → maintain awareness
Exam pearls
The three elements
IQ < 70 + impaired adaptive/social functioning + onset before adulthood (lifelong) — IQ alone is not enough.
Not to be confused
LD ≠ learning difficulty (dyslexia = specific, not global); LD ≠ acquired cognitive impairment (dementia/brain injury in adulthood).
Severity
Mild (50–69, majority, often independent), moderate (35–49), severe (20–34), profound (<20).
Causes
Down's, Fragile X (commonest inherited), PKU, fetal alcohol syndrome, birth asphyxia, congenital infection.
Comorbidities
Epilepsy, autism, ADHD, mental illness, sensory/physical disability; behaviour that challenges often signals pain/distress/unmet need → find the cause.
Diagnostic overshadowing
Wrongly attributing symptoms to the LD instead of investigating → major cause of avoidable death.
Reasonable adjustments
Equality Act 2010 legal duty; hospital passport, annual health check (14+), easy-read info, longer appointments.
Policy concepts
STOMP/STAMP (stop over-medication), LeDeR (mortality reviews), Oliver McGowan training.
Capacity
LD does NOT equal lacking capacity — presume capacity, assess decision-specifically (cross-ref MCA).
Behaviour that challenges
Treat the cause + Positive Behaviour Support first, not antipsychotics.
PSYCHIATRY__Sleep Disorders:
Overview — What & why
A group of conditions that disrupt the quantity, quality, or timing of sleep, or produce abnormal events during sleep — with major impact on mood, cognition and physical health.
The core concept: sleep disorders sort into a few categories — can't sleep (insomnia), can't stay awake (hypersomnias/narcolepsy), abnormal events (parasomnias), disordered breathing (OSA), abnormal movements (RLS), mistimed sleep (circadian). Placing the complaint in the right category is the whole diagnostic step.
Common; frequently comorbid with psychiatric illness (depression, anxiety, PTSD) — insomnia both causes and results from mental illness.
The decisive fork — which category?
Category Core complaint Examples
Insomniacan't fall/stay asleepchronic insomnia disorder
Hypersomniaexcessive daytime sleepiness despite adequate opportunitynarcolepsy, idiopathic hypersomnia
Parasomniasabnormal events during sleepsleepwalking, night terrors, RBD, sleep paralysis, nightmares
Sleep-related breathingsnoring + apnoeas + daytime sleepinessobstructive sleep apnoea (OSA)
Movement disordersurge to move / abnormal movementsrestless legs syndrome (RLS), periodic limb movements
Circadian rhythmsleep at the wrong time (timing, not quality)delayed sleep phase, shift-work, jet lag
Sleep architecture (the physiology anchor)
  • Sleep cycles between non-REM (N1–N3, including deep slow-wave sleep) and REM sleep (dreaming, with physiological muscle atonia)
  • Non-REM parasomnias (sleepwalking, night terrors) arise from deep slow-wave sleep → early in the night, no dream recall, common in children
  • REM parasomnias (nightmares, sleep paralysis, REM sleep behaviour disorder) arise from REM → later in the night, dream-related
Cross-ref neurophysiology — REM atonia is the normal paralysis that sleep paralysis and RBD both relate to.
Insomnia (the commonest)
Difficulty falling or staying asleep, with daytime impairment, despite adequate opportunity to sleep. Chronic insomnia = symptoms ≥3 nights/week for ≥3 months (acute/short-term is <3 months, often stress-related).
Causes / associations
  • Psychiatric: depression, anxiety (very common — early morning waking suggests depression)
  • Physical: pain, nocturia, respiratory
  • Substances: caffeine, alcohol, stimulants
  • Poor sleep hygiene; other sleep disorders (OSA, RLS)
Assessment: history + sleep diary, bed-partner collateral, screen for depression/anxiety and for OSA/RLS, medication/substance review.
Management (NICE/CKS):
  • 1. Sleep hygiene + address the cause (treat depression/pain, cut caffeine/alcohol, regular routine)
  • 2. CBT for insomnia (CBT-i) = first-line treatment for chronic insomnia — the key modern point: CBT-i, not drugs, is first-line
  • 3. Short-term hypnotic only if severe/acute: a z-drug (zopiclone, zolpidem) or short-acting benzodiazepine, lowest dose, shortest time (≤2 weeks) — dependence, tolerance, falls
Melatonin — an option in adults ≥55 (short-term). Daridorexant (dual orexin receptor antagonist, NICE TA922) — for long-term insomnia where CBT-i has failed/is unavailable. Principle: avoid long-term hypnotics; drugs are a temporary adjunct.
Narcolepsy (the classic hypersomnia)
Chronic excessive daytime sleepiness with sudden sleep attacks, caused by loss of orexin (hypocretin) signalling — the wakefulness neuropeptide.
Tetrad feature Detail
Excessive daytime sleepinessirresistible sleep attacks (the core)
Cataplexysudden loss of muscle tone triggered by emotion (e.g. laughter) — highly specific to narcolepsy type 1
Sleep paralysistransient paralysis on waking/falling asleep
Hypnagogic hallucinationsvivid hallucinations at sleep onset
Mechanism link: loss of orexin → intrusion of REM phenomena into wakefulness (cataplexy, sleep paralysis, hallucinations are all REM-atonia/dream elements breaking through).
Diagnosis: sleep studies + Multiple Sleep Latency Test (MSLT); low CSF orexin. Management: sleep hygiene + scheduled naps; stimulants (modafinil) for sleepiness; SSRIs/SNRIs or sodium oxybate for cataplexy.
Parasomnias (abnormal events in sleep)
Parasomnia Sleep stage Features
Sleep paralysisREM-relatedtransient paralysis of skeletal muscles on waking (or falling asleep), ± hallucinations; the normal REM atonia persisting into wakefulness; common/benign
Night terrorsnon-REM (deep)sudden arousal with terror, screaming, autonomic surge; child not fully awake, no memory; early night; childhood
Sleepwalkingnon-REM (deep)complex behaviours while asleep; no memory; childhood
NightmaresREMfrightening dreams with recall; later night
REM sleep behaviour disorder (RBD)REMloss of normal REM atonia → acting out dreams (punching, kicking); strongly associated with future α-synucleinopathies (Parkinson's, DLB)
RBD high-yield: often precedes Parkinson's/DLB by years (cross-ref dementia + basal ganglia notes).
Night terrors vs nightmares: night terrors = non-REM, early night, no recall, child not woken; nightmares = REM, later night, recalled.
Sleep paralysis management: reassurance; clonazepam if troublesome/frequent.
Obstructive sleep apnoea (OSA)
Repeated upper-airway collapse during sleep → apnoeas/hypopnoeas → repeated arousals → fragmented sleep.
Features & risk factors
  • Loud snoring, witnessed apnoeas (bed-partner report)
  • Excessive daytime sleepiness, morning headache, poor concentration
  • Risk: obesity, large neck, male, alcohol
Assessment & management
  • Epworth Sleepiness Scale, sleep study (polysomnography)
  • Weight loss, avoid alcohol/sedatives
  • CPAP (first-line moderate–severe); mandibular devices
  • DVLA implications (must not drive if sleepiness affects driving)
Consequences: hypertension, cardiovascular disease, road-traffic accidents.
Restless legs syndrome (RLS)
Irresistible urge to move the legs, worse at rest/evening, relieved by movement, disrupting sleep.
  • Associations: iron deficiency (check ferritin — reversible), pregnancy, renal failure, neuropathy
  • Management: treat iron deficiency; sleep hygiene; dopamine agonists (ropinirole, pramipexole) or gabapentinoids if severe
Circadian rhythm disorders
  • Sleep occurs at the wrong time (the sleep itself is normal): delayed sleep phase (common in adolescents), shift-work disorder, jet lag
  • Management: sleep scheduling, timed light exposure, melatonin
Exam pearls
Categorise first
Insomnia (can't sleep) vs hypersomnia/narcolepsy (can't stay awake) vs parasomnia (events in sleep) vs OSA (snoring + apnoeas) vs RLS (urge to move) vs circadian (wrong timing).
Chronic insomnia
≥3 nights/week for ≥3 months; CBT-i first-line (not drugs); short-term z-drug/benzodiazepine only (≤2 weeks); melatonin ≥55; daridorexant if CBT-i fails.
Narcolepsy tetrad
Excessive sleepiness + cataplexy (emotion-triggered atonia) + sleep paralysis + hypnagogic hallucinations; orexin loss → REM intrusion; modafinil for sleepiness.
Parasomnias by stage
Non-REM (early night, no recall) = night terrors + sleepwalking (children); REM (recalled) = nightmares, sleep paralysis, RBD.
Sleep paralysis
REM atonia intruding on wakefulness → reassurance, clonazepam if troublesome.
RBD
Acting out dreams → precedes Parkinson's/DLB.
OSA
Loud snoring + witnessed apnoeas + daytime sleepiness → Epworth + sleep study → CPAP; DVLA implications.
RLS
Urge to move, worse at rest, relieved by movement → check ferritin (iron deficiency); dopamine agonists if severe.
PSYCHIATRY__Dementias (psychiatric frami:
Overview — What & why
Dementia = an acquired, chronic, usually progressive decline in cognition (memory, language, executive function, personality) severe enough to impair daily function, occurring in clear consciousness.
The core concept — a three-step framework: (1) is it dementia at all, or a mimic (delirium, depression)? → (2) which subtype? → (3) manage cognition + BPSD + risk. The mimics matter most because delirium and depression are reversible and must not be mislabelled as dementia.
Huge overlap with psychiatry via BPSD (behavioural & psychological symptoms of dementia — agitation, psychosis, depression, sleep disturbance).
First fork — dementia vs its two great mimics
Dementia Delirium Depression (pseudodementia)
Onsetinsidious (months–years)acute (hours–days)subacute (weeks)
Courseprogressive, stable day-to-dayfluctuating (worse at night)relatively stable
Consciousness/attentionclear (attention preserved early)clouded, inattentive (hallmark)clear
Memoryearly loss, patient often unconcernedpoor registration"don't know" answers, patient worried
Reversible?usually notyes (treat the cause)yes (treat the depression)
The rules: acute + fluctuating + inattentive + clouded → DELIRIUM (exclude first); short history + biological symptoms + patient distressed about memory + "don't know" answers + global loss → DEPRESSION (pseudodementia); insidious + progressive + clear consciousness + patient unconcerned → DEMENTIA.
Second fork — which subtype?
Dementia Onset/course Distinguishing features Pathology
Alzheimer's (~60%)insidious, gradualearly memory loss (the 4 A's)amyloid plaques + tau tangles; ↓ACh
Vascular (2nd)stepwisepatchy deficits, focal neurology, vascular risk factorscerebrovascular disease
DLBfluctuatingfluctuating cognition + visual hallucinations + parkinsonism + REM sleep behaviour disorderα-synuclein (Lewy bodies)
Frontotemporal (<65)insidiousearly personality/behaviour change + language impairment, memory spared earlytau (Pick bodies) / TDP-43
Discriminators: Alzheimer's = memory first, gradual; vascular = stepwise + vascular risk factors; DLB = fluctuating + visual hallucinations + parkinsonism; FTD = personality/language first, memory spared early (younger).
Alzheimer's disease (the commonest)
Early, prominent memory loss (recent memories lost first), gradually progressing to global cognitive decline.
The 4 A's (high-yield mnemonic):
A Meaning
Amnesiarecent memories lost first
Aphasiaword-finding difficulty, muddled/disjointed speech
Agnosiarecognition problems (faces, objects)
Apraxiacan't carry out skilled tasks despite normal motor function
Pathology: extracellular amyloid-β plaques + intracellular tau neurofibrillary tangles; cholinergic deficit (↓acetylcholine) → the rationale for acetylcholinesterase inhibitors (cross-ref the synaptic transmission / ACh note).
Vascular dementia
Cognitive impairment from cerebrovascular disease, classically stepwise progression (each "step" = a further vascular insult), often with focal neurology and vascular risk factors (hypertension, diabetes, AF, smoking).
  • Subtypes: post-stroke, subcortical small-vessel, and mixed (with Alzheimer's — common)
  • Management emphasis: control cardiovascular risk factors (the modifiable part), symptomatic treatment, advance care planning
Dementia with Lewy bodies (DLB)
The core triad: fluctuating cognition + recurrent visual hallucinations + spontaneous parkinsonism (bradykinesia, rigidity, tremor).
  • Also: REM sleep behaviour disorder (acting out dreams — often precedes it by years), autonomic dysfunction, repeated falls
  • Pathology: α-synuclein (Lewy bodies) — the same protein as Parkinson's (cross-ref basal ganglia / Parkinson's note)
  • DLB vs Parkinson's disease dementia — the "1-year rule": dementia before or within 1 year of parkinsonism → DLB; parkinsonism preceding dementia by >1 year → Parkinson's disease dementia
CRITICAL — antipsychotic sensitivity: people with DLB can have severe, sometimes fatal reactions to antipsychotics (worsening parkinsonism, sedation, NMS-like reactions) → AVOID antipsychotics if at all possible; if essential, use the lowest dose of an atypical with extreme caution.
Frontotemporal dementia (FTD / Pick's)
Early personality and behaviour change (disinhibition, apathy, loss of empathy, compulsive behaviours) and/or language impairment (progressive aphasia) — with memory relatively preserved early (the key contrast with Alzheimer's).
  • Younger onset (often <65)
  • Pathology: Pick bodies (accumulation of tau protein within neurones) / TDP-43
Management point: do NOT give acetylcholinesterase inhibitors or memantine in FTD (no benefit, may worsen).
Investigations (confirm dementia + exclude reversible causes)
  • Cognitive assessment: bedside screening (MMSE, MoCA, 6-CIT, AMTS); formal neuropsychology if needed
  • Bloods to exclude reversible causes (essential): FBC, U&E, LFT, TFT (hypothyroidism), calcium, glucose/HbA1c, B12 + folate; HIV/syphilis if indicated
  • Medication review (anticholinergic burden worsens cognition)
  • Neuroimaging (MRI preferred): exclude structural causes (tumour, subdural, normal pressure hydrocephalus), assess atrophy/vascular load; DAT scan supports DLB (↓dopamine transporter uptake)
  • Depression screen (exclude pseudodementia)
Management (NICE NG97)
Overarching principle: subtype-specific cognitive drugs + non-drug-first management of BPSD + support, advance care planning, and cardiovascular risk control.
Subtype Drug management (NICE)
Alzheimer's1st-line mild–moderate: acetylcholinesterase inhibitor (donepezil, galantamine, rivastigmine); memantine (NMDA antagonist) for severe, or moderate if AChEi not tolerated, or add-on
DLBAChE inhibitors (donepezil/rivastigmine) — often effective (marked cholinergic deficit); memantine if not tolerated
Vascularcontrol cardiovascular risk factors; AChEi/memantine only if suspected comorbid Alzheimer's/DLB/PD dementia
FTDdo NOT use AChE inhibitors or memantine
AChE inhibitor caution: avoid/caution with QT prolongation, bradycardia, cardiac conduction problems (pro-cholinergic → bradycardia) → in QT prolongation, use cognitive stimulation therapy instead. Re-titrate rivastigmine/galantamine if >3 days missed.
BPSD — psychiatric management
  • Non-pharmacological FIRST: identify triggers (pain, infection, constipation, environment), person-centred approaches, cognitive stimulation, structured activity
  • Antipsychotics ONLY if severe distress or risk to self/others and non-drug measures have failed — short-term, lowest dose (e.g. risperidone)
  • Risk: antipsychotics ↑stroke + ↑mortality in elderly dementia → use sparingly, review regularly
  • DLB: avoid antipsychotics (severe sensitivity)
Supportive (all dementias)
  • Psychoeducation + carer support, occupational therapy, structured routine
  • Advance care planning, Lasting Power of Attorney, capacity assessments (cross-ref MHA/capacity)
  • Treat comorbid depression; DVLA notification; safeguarding
Exam pearls
Exclude reversible mimics first
Delirium (acute, fluctuating, inattentive, clouded) and depression/pseudodementia (short history, biological symptoms, patient worried about memory, "don't know" answers, global loss).
Alzheimer's
Memory first, gradual — 4 A's: Amnesia, Aphasia, Agnosia, Apraxia.
Vascular
Stepwise + vascular risk factors → control cardiovascular risk.
DLB
Fluctuating + visual hallucinations + parkinsonism (+ REM sleep behaviour disorder); 1-year rule vs PD dementia.
FTD
Early personality/language change, memory spared, younger; Pick bodies (tau). NO AChEi/memantine.
Pathology
Alzheimer's = amyloid plaques + tau tangles (↓ACh); DLB = α-synuclein (Lewy bodies); FTD = tau (Pick bodies).
DLB antipsychotic sensitivity
Severe/fatal reactions → AVOID antipsychotics; use AChE inhibitors for cognition.
Management
Alzheimer's → AChE inhibitor (donepezil) 1st-line, memantine for severe; vascular → cardiovascular risk control; FTD → none.
BPSD
Non-drug first; antipsychotics only short-term for severe distress/risk (↑stroke + ↑mortality).
AChE inhibitors
Caution in bradycardia/QT prolongation (pro-cholinergic).
Investigations
Cognitive screen + bloods to exclude reversible causes (TFT, B12, calcium) + MRI + medication review.
PSYCHIATRY__Substance Use Disorder:
Overview — What & why
Substance use disorder = a pattern of substance use leading to dependence, harm, or impaired control, despite negative consequences.
The core concept: identify the substance and, for each, separate the three clinical problems that need different management: (1) intoxication/overdose, (2) withdrawal, (3) long-term dependence/relapse prevention. Getting the substance × problem grid right is the whole framework.
Epidemiology: major cause of morbidity/mortality; high comorbidity with depression, anxiety, PTSD and personality disorder.
The decisive fork — which substance, which problem?
Substance Intoxication / overdose Withdrawal Long-term (dependence)
Alcoholdisinhibition, ataxia, slurred speech; coma/resp depression if severethe dangerous one — tremor → seizures → delirium tremensacamprosate / naltrexone / disulfiram + psychosocial
Opioids↓consciousness, ↓RR, pinpoint pupils → naloxoneunpleasant but not life-threatening (flu-like)methadone / buprenorphine substitution; naltrexone
Stimulantsagitation, ↑HR/BP, mydriasis, MI/stroke risk, psychosisdysphoria, fatigue ("crash")psychological (no substitution)
Benzodiazepinessedation, resp depression (esp. with alcohol/opioids) → flumazenil (rarely)like alcohol — seizures, potentially dangerousgradual dose reduction (long-acting)
Two high-yield contrasts: alcohol + benzodiazepine withdrawal = dangerous (seizures, delirium) → needs medically-assisted withdrawal; opioid withdrawal = miserable but rarely life-threatening, whereas opioid overdose = the killer (respiratory depression).
Dependence — the general concept (applies across substances)
Features of dependence (ICD framework)
  • Strong desire/compulsion to use (craving)
  • Impaired control over use (amount/duration)
  • Tolerance (needing more for the same effect)
  • Withdrawal state on stopping (± using to relieve it)
  • Salience — the substance takes priority; neglect of other interests; persistent use despite harm
Memory anchor: craving · control loss · tolerance · withdrawal · salience · persistence despite harm.
Alcohol withdrawal — the mechanism
Chronic alcohol enhances GABA (inhibitory) + inhibits NMDA/glutamate (excitatory) → the CNS adapts by downregulating GABA + upregulating NMDA. On stopping, the adaptation is unopposed → CNS hyperexcitability (↓inhibition + ↑excitation) → withdrawal, dominated by sympathetic overactivity.
Cross-ref the synaptic transmission / GABA note — this is why benzodiazepines (which boost GABA) are the treatment.
Alcohol withdrawal — the timeline
Time after last drink Feature
6–12 hourstremor, sweating, tachycardia, anxiety, nausea
~12–24 hoursalcoholic hallucinosis (classically auditory, in clear consciousness — visual hallucinations instead suggest delirium tremens)
~36 hourspeak seizure risk ("rum fits")
48–72 hoursdelirium tremens
Delirium tremens (DTs): coarse tremor, confusion/delirium, agitation, visual hallucinations, delusions, fever, tachycardia, autonomic instability — a medical emergency (mortality if untreated).
Alcohol withdrawal — management
  • Assisted withdrawal with a long-acting benzodiazepine — chlordiazepoxide (first-line) or diazepam, in a reducing regimen over ~5–7 days
  • Use lorazepam in significant liver impairment (less accumulation)
  • Regimen: symptom-triggered (dose to severity, e.g. CIWA-Ar) or fixed reducing-dose
  • DTs: benzodiazepines (oral or parenteral); rescue with parenteral lorazepam; haloperidol only as an adjunct for agitation/hallucinations alongside benzodiazepines
  • Withdrawal seizures: benzodiazepines (no long-term anticonvulsant needed)
  • Admit if history of complex/severe withdrawal, seizures, or DTs
ALWAYS give thiamine (Pabrinex) to prevent Wernicke's — and before glucose (cross-ref the Wernicke's note).
Alcohol dependence — relapse prevention
After withdrawal, maintain abstinence with psychosocial support + a relapse-prevention drug:
Drug Mechanism Notes
Acamprosatemodulates glutamate/GABA → ↓cravinggood in hepatic impairment; start after abstinence achieved
Naltrexoneopioid antagonist → ↓the reward of drinkingavoid in opioid users (precipitates withdrawal); caution in liver disease
Disulfiraminhibits aldehyde dehydrogenase → acetaldehyde builds up → unpleasant reaction (flushing, vomiting, headache) if alcohol takena deterrent; needs a motivated patient; avoid in cardiac disease
Also: motivational interviewing/CBT, mutual-aid (AA), treat comorbid depression/anxiety, ongoing thiamine if still drinking. Cross-ref the alcoholic liver disease note.
Opioid overdose (the emergency)
Triad: ↓consciousness + ↓respiratory rate + pinpoint pupils (miosis).
  • Management: NALOXONE (opioid antagonist) — titrate to respiratory function
  • Short half-life → may need repeat doses/infusion (patient can re-sedate)
  • Take-home naloxone for at-risk patients
Cross-ref opioid pharmacology — respiratory depression is the fatal effect.
Opioid withdrawal (unpleasant, not usually dangerous)
Flu-like: agitation, sweating, rhinorrhoea, lacrimation, yawning, dilated pupils (mydriasis), abdominal cramps, diarrhoea, piloerection, myalgia.
Management (symptomatic + substitution)
  • NICE advises against prescribing opioids purely to manage withdrawal where symptomatic treatment/lofexidine suffices
  • Lofexidine (α2-agonist) — for withdrawal symptoms
  • Loperamide (diarrhoea), antiemetics (nausea), benzodiazepines (agitation)
Opioid dependence — substitution & relapse prevention
  • Detox/maintenance: methadone (full agonist; prolongs QTc) OR buprenorphine (partial agonist — can precipitate withdrawal if given too soon after a full agonist, so start once in withdrawal)
  • Relapse prevention after detox: naltrexone (opioid antagonist — blocks the effect of opioids)
  • Overdose: naloxone (as above)
  • Harm reduction: needle exchange, blood-borne virus testing (HIV, hepatitis B/C), vaccination
Stimulants & other substances
Stimulants (cocaine, amphetamines)
  • Intoxication → agitation, ↑HR/BP, mydriasis, hyperthermia, risk of MI/stroke/arrhythmia, and stimulant psychosis
  • No substitution therapy — management is supportive + psychological; benzodiazepines for agitation
Cannabis
  • Dependence; anxiety/psychosis risk
  • Psychological management
Benzodiazepines
  • Dependence common; withdrawal like alcohol (seizures)
  • Gradual reduction — switch to a long-acting agent (e.g. diazepam), then taper
Assessment
  • History: substance(s), quantity/frequency, route, duration, features of dependence, previous withdrawal (seizures/DTs), overdose history, injecting, blood-borne virus risk, forensic/social context
  • Screening tools: CAGE, AUDIT (alcohol); SADQ (severity of alcohol dependence); CIWA-Ar (withdrawal severity)
  • Examination + bloods: signs of chronic use/liver disease; FBC, U&E, LFT + GGT, clotting, glucose, blood-borne virus screen (HIV, hepatitis B/C); ↑MCV and ↑GGT suggest chronic alcohol use
  • Screen for comorbid mental illness and risk (self-harm/suicide — cross-ref)
Exam pearls
Framework
For each substance separate intoxication/overdose vs withdrawal vs long-term dependence.
Danger map
Alcohol/benzo withdrawal = dangerous (seizures, DTs); opioid withdrawal = miserable but rarely fatal; opioid overdose = the killer.
Alcohol withdrawal mechanism
↑GABA/↓NMDA adaptation → unopposed CNS excitation on stopping → treat with benzodiazepines (chlordiazepoxide; lorazepam if liver failure).
Withdrawal timeline
Tremor/anxiety 6–12h → seizures ~36h → delirium tremens 48–72h (coarse tremor, confusion, hallucinations, fever, autonomic instability).
Thiamine
Always give thiamine (before glucose) in alcohol withdrawal → prevents Wernicke's.
Alcohol relapse prevention
Acamprosate (↓craving, good in liver disease), naltrexone (↓reward), disulfiram (deterrent — acetaldehyde reaction).
Opioid overdose
↓GCS + ↓RR + pinpoint pupils → naloxone (short half-life, may repeat).
Opioid substitution
Methadone (full agonist, ↑QTc) or buprenorphine (partial agonist — precipitates withdrawal if given too early); naltrexone for relapse prevention post-detox.
Buprenorphine
Partial agonist — start once withdrawing; stimulants have NO substitution therapy.
PSYCHIATRY__Somatisation / Medically Une:
Overview — What & why
A group of disorders where physical symptoms cause distress/impairment but are not fully explained by organic disease — or where the psychological response to symptoms is disproportionate. They sit at the interface of mind and body.
The core concept: two questions organise the whole group — (1) is the patient consciously producing/feigning the symptoms? and (2) if feigning, is there external gain? These two questions separate every diagnosis below.
Epidemiology: common in primary/secondary care; high comorbidity with depression and anxiety; associated with past trauma/adversity. Terminology: DSM-5 renamed these the "somatic symptom and related disorders" — modern names are given alongside the classic ones below.
The decisive fork — conscious production, and is there external gain?
The exam discriminator. Two yes/no questions place any patient:
Unconsciously produced (genuine, not feigned) Consciously feigned/produced
No external gainSomatic symptom disorder, illness anxiety disorder, functional neurological disorderFactitious disorder (gain is the sick role itself — internal/psychological)
External gain present—Malingering (gain is external: money, drugs, time off, avoiding prison)
The rule (high-yield):
• Not consciously produced → somatoform group — the patient is NOT faking
• Consciously produced + gain is the sick role → factitious disorder (Munchausen's)
• Consciously produced + external/tangible gain → malingering (not a psychiatric diagnosis — deception for reward)
Key axis: factitious and malingering both involve deliberate feigning — they differ only in the motive (sick role vs external reward). The somatoform group is genuinely experienced.
The somatoform disorders (unconsciously produced — NOT faking)
Disorder (modern name) Old name Core feature Discriminator
Somatic symptom disordersomatisation disordermultiple physical symptoms (across systems) + disproportionate thoughts/anxiety/behaviour about them, persisting (>6 months); symptoms are real and distressingfocus is on the symptoms themselves (recurrent, multi-system); classically ≥2 years without organic cause
Illness anxiety disorderhypochondriasisexcessive preoccupation with having a serious illness (e.g. cancer), despite minimal or no actual symptoms; "doctor shopping"focus is on the fear of having a disease (not the symptoms) — few/no symptoms, lots of worry
Functional neurological disorder (FND)conversion disorderneurological symptoms (motor/sensory loss, weakness, non-epileptic seizures, blindness) incompatible with organic disease, often after a stressor; not consciously producedgenuine neurological deficit with positive signs of incompatibility (e.g. Hoover's sign); patient is NOT faking
Somatic symptom vs illness anxiety (high-yield): somatic symptom disorder = distress about real symptoms (many, multi-system); illness anxiety disorder = fear of having a disease with few/no symptoms ("doctor shopping").
Hoover's sign (high-yield): a rule-in sign for functional (non-organic) leg weakness. When the patient lifts the unaffected leg against resistance, you feel involuntary downward pressure (hip extension) in the "paralysed" leg that was absent on direct testing — demonstrating the motor pathway is intact and the weakness is functional, not organic.
The feigned disorders (consciously produced — the patient IS faking)
Disorder Motive Key point
Factitious disorder (Munchausen's syndrome)the sick role itself (internal/psychological gain — to be a patient, receive care)deliberately fakes/induces symptoms (e.g. injecting insulin, contaminating samples) but for no external reward
Malingeringexternal gain (money, benefits, drugs, time off, avoiding prosecution)NOT a psychiatric disorder — intentional feigning for tangible reward
Factitious disorder imposed on another (formerly Munchausen's by proxy): fabricating/inducing illness in another person (usually a child) → a safeguarding emergency (child protection).
Factitious vs malingering: both feign deliberately; factitious = wants to be sick (sick role); malingering = wants a reward.
Assessment (a careful, respectful approach)
  • Exclude organic disease appropriately — but avoid over-investigating (repeated tests reinforce illness behaviour and cause iatrogenic harm)
  • Full history including psychosocial context, stressors, past trauma, and previous presentations (a pattern of multiple unexplained presentations is itself informative)
  • Look for positive functional signs where relevant (e.g. Hoover's sign in functional leg weakness, inconsistency in non-epileptic seizures)
  • Screen for comorbid depression and anxiety (very common and treatable)
  • Do not confuse "no organic cause found" with "faking" — the somatoform disorders are genuinely experienced; the diagnosis is positive, not merely one of exclusion
Management (general principles — largely shared)
Overarching principle: a single, trusted clinician, limited investigation, validation of distress, and treatment of comorbidity — not repeated referral/testing.
Shared approach (somatoform group)
  • One consistent clinician/GP to coordinate care (reduces doctor-shopping); regular scheduled reviews rather than symptom-driven
  • Validate the symptoms as real and distressing while gently reframing toward a biopsychosocial understanding
  • Limit unnecessary investigations and referrals (avoid reinforcing illness behaviour + iatrogenic harm)
  • CBT is the psychological mainstay (somatic symptom disorder, illness anxiety, FND)
  • FND: clear positive explanation + physiotherapy (functional motor symptoms) + MDT input
  • Treat comorbid depression/anxiety (e.g. SSRI + psychological therapy) — often the highest-yield intervention
Feigned disorders
  • Factitious disorder: difficult to manage; avoid confrontation, minimise harm from investigations, involve psychiatry
  • Malingering: not treated as an illness; manage the situation (don't provide the sought secondary gain), but consider genuine comorbidity
  • Factitious disorder imposed on another: safeguarding referral (child protection) is the priority
Exam pearls
Two organising questions
(1) consciously produced? (2) external gain? — these place every diagnosis.
Somatoform group
Not consciously produced → patient NOT faking (somatic symptom, illness anxiety, FND).
Factitious vs malingering
Both feign; factitious = sick role (internal); malingering = external reward (not a psychiatric diagnosis).
Somatic symptom disorder
Distress about multiple real symptoms (multi-system, ≥2 years / >6 months).
Illness anxiety disorder
(old: hypochondriasis) fear of having a serious illness with few/no symptoms — "doctor shopping".
Functional neurological disorder
(old: conversion disorder) deficit incompatible with organic disease, often post-stressor, not feigned → Hoover's sign rules in functional leg weakness.
Munchausen's by proxy
Factitious disorder imposed on another = safeguarding emergency.
Management
One trusted clinician, limit investigations, validate distress, CBT, treat comorbid depression/anxiety; FND → positive explanation + physiotherapy.
PSYCHIATRY__Personality Disorders:
Overview — What & why
A personality disorder is an enduring, pervasive pattern of inner experience and behaviour that deviates markedly from cultural expectations, is stable over time, and causes distress or functional impairment.
The core concept: unlike episodic illnesses (depression, psychosis), a personality disorder is a long-standing trait pattern — present since adolescence/early adulthood, across situations, rather than a discrete episode. This is what distinguishes it from a state/Axis I disorder.
Epidemiology: emerge by late adolescence/early adulthood; high comorbidity with mood, anxiety and substance disorders, and self-harm.
The decisive fork — which of the three clusters?
📷 Image placeholder — Three-cluster map — A odd/eccentric (paranoid/schizoid/schizotypal), B dramatic/erratic (antisocial/borderline/histrionic/narcissistic), C anxious/fearful (avoidant/dependent/obsessive-compulsive)
The ten personality disorders group into three clusters by their dominant flavour — the single most useful classification:
Cluster Theme Memory hook Disorders
AOdd / eccentric"Weird" (Mad)Paranoid, Schizoid, Schizotypal
BDramatic / emotional / erratic"Wild" (Bad)Antisocial, Borderline (EUPD), Histrionic, Narcissistic
CAnxious / fearful"Worried" (Sad)Avoidant, Dependent, Obsessive-Compulsive PD
Rule of thumb: A = odd (relate poorly, "schizophrenia-like" spectrum); B = dramatic (impulsive, emotional, interpersonal chaos); C = anxious (fear-driven). — "Weird, Wild, Worried" / "Mad, Bad, Sad".
Cluster A — odd / eccentric (the "schizophrenia-spectrum" flavour)
Disorder Key features Discriminator
Paranoidpervasive distrust/suspiciousness, questions others' loyalty, reluctant to confide, bears grudges, reads hidden threatening meaningssuspicion without psychosis or magical thinking
Schizoiddetachment + emotional coldness — prefers solitude, few friends, indifferent to praise/criticism, little interest in sex/relationships"schizOID = devOID of emotion/interest" — the negative symptoms of schizophrenia, without psychosis

Cluster A discriminators: schizoid = withdrawn + emotionally cold (no desire for contact); schizotypal = odd + magical thinking + eccentric (the "almost-psychotic" one); paranoid = suspicious. Schizotypal's ideas of reference differ from delusions in that insight is retained.
Cluster B — dramatic / emotional / erratic
Disorder Key features Discriminator
Antisocialdisregard for others' rights + social norms — repeated law-breaking, deceit, impulsivity, no remorse, irritability/aggression, irresponsibility♂ > ♀; lack of remorse + rule-breaking; must be ≥18 (conduct disorder before)

Cluster B discriminators: antisocial = no remorse/breaks rules; borderline = unstable + self-harm + fear of abandonment; histrionic = attention-seeking/theatrical; narcissistic = grandiose + entitled. Borderline has the self-harm and emptiness; histrionic is more purely attention-seeking without the self-destructive instability.
Cluster C — anxious / fearful
📷 Image placeholder — Ego-syntonic vs ego-dystonic — OCPD (traits felt as correct, no true obsessions/compulsions) vs OCD (distressing intrusive obsessions + compulsions the patient wants rid of)
Disorder Key features Discriminator
Avoidantfear of criticism/rejection — avoids interpersonal/occupational contact, feels inept/inferior, won't engage unless certain of being likedwants relationships but fear holds them back
Dependentexcessive need to be cared for — submissive, clinging, can't make decisions alone, urgently seeks a new relationship when one ends, lacks self-confidence/initiativecan't function without others' support
