Cluster C discriminators: avoidant = wants contact but fears rejection; dependent = needs others to take responsibility; OCPD = rigid perfectionist.
OCPD vs OCD (critical): OCPD = an ego-syntonic personality trait (rigid perfectionism/orderliness the person sees as correct — no true obsessions/compulsions); OCD = an ego-dystonic anxiety disorder with intrusive obsessions + compulsions the person finds distressing and wants rid of.
Assessment (largely clinical)
  • Clinical diagnosis — an enduring, pervasive pattern present since adolescence/early adulthood, across multiple situations, causing distress/impairment; a longitudinal history + collateral is essential
  • Exclude a state/Axis I disorder better explaining the picture (depression, psychosis, bipolar, substance use) and organic causes
  • Always screen for comorbid depression, anxiety, substance misuse, and self-harm/suicide risk (especially borderline)
  • Note: ICD-11 has moved toward a dimensional "severity + traits" model, but the cluster/type framework remains how they're taught and examined
Management
Overarching principle: psychological therapy is the mainstay; drugs are NOT used to treat the personality disorder itself.
Psychological therapy = mainstay
  • Dialectical behaviour therapy (DBT) — best-evidenced, especially for borderline PD (NICE: consider a comprehensive DBT programme for women with borderline PD where reducing recurrent self-harm is a priority)
  • Other structured therapies: mentalisation-based therapy (MBT), cognitive/schema-focused therapy, therapeutic communities
Drug treatment (high-yield NICE point): do NOT use drugs specifically to treat borderline PD or its individual symptoms; antipsychotics should not be used for medium/long-term treatment. Drugs are only for comorbid conditions (e.g. depression, anxiety). A short-term sedative may be considered cautiously in a crisis — for no longer than ~1 week.
Setting & antisocial PD
  • Treat in the community where possible; avoid long unstructured hospital admissions (can worsen borderline PD)
  • Antisocial PD: manage risk; limited treatment response; address comorbid substance use; structured psychological programmes where appropriate
Exam pearls
Trait, not episode
Enduring, pervasive pattern from early adulthood — distinguishes it from depression/psychosis.
Three clusters
A = odd (Paranoid, Schizoid, Schizotypal); B = dramatic (Antisocial, Borderline, Histrionic, Narcissistic); C = anxious (Avoidant, Dependent, OCPD). "Weird, Wild, Worried" / "Mad, Bad, Sad".
Cluster A
Schizoid = devoid of emotion/interest (negative-symptom-like); schizotypal = odd + magical thinking + ideas of reference WITH insight.
Borderline (EUPD)
Fear of abandonment + unstable relationships (idealisation↔devaluation) + self-harm + emptiness.
Rest of Cluster B
Antisocial = no remorse + breaks rules (♂); narcissistic = grandiose + entitled + no empathy; histrionic = attention-seeking.
OCPD ≠ OCD
OCPD = ego-syntonic rigid perfectionism (a trait); OCD = ego-dystonic obsessions + compulsions (an anxiety disorder).
Management
Psychological therapy (DBT best-evidenced, esp. borderline); do NOT treat the disorder with drugs; antipsychotics not for medium/long-term; short-term sedative in crisis only (≤1 week).
Safety & setting
Always screen borderline PD for self-harm/suicide risk; treat in the community, avoid long admissions.
PSYCHIATRY__Eating Disorders (anorexia,:
Overview — What & why
Eating disorders are psychiatric illnesses with prominent physical consequences — disturbed eating behaviour with an over-valuation of weight/shape (anorexia, bulimia) or restricted intake (ARFID).
The core concept: these are serious medical as well as psychiatric conditions — anorexia nervosa has the highest mortality of any psychiatric disorder (medical complications + suicide). Recognition of physical risk sits alongside the psychological diagnosis.
Epidemiology: predominantly adolescents/young adults; commoner in females; high comorbidity with depression, anxiety and OCD.
The decisive fork — which eating disorder?
Distinguished by weight, the presence of binge/purge, and the driving belief:
Anorexia nervosa Bulimia nervosa ARFID
Weightlow (restriction → underweight)usually normal / slightly highlow/normal (inadequate intake)
Core behaviourrestriction ± excessive exercise (± purging)binge + compensatory purging (vomiting, laxatives, diuretics, exercise)avoidant/restrictive intake
Driving belieffear of weight gain + distorted body imagefear of weight gain + over-valuation of shape/weightNOT body image — sensory aversion, fear of aversive consequences (choking), or low interest in food
Key signlow weight + physical sequelaenormal weight + purging signs (Russell's, dental erosion)nutritional deficiency / failure to gain, no body-image disturbance
The rule (high-yield): anorexia = low weight + body-image disturbance; bulimia = normal weight + binge-purge cycle; ARFID = restricted intake WITHOUT body-image concern (its distinguishing feature).
Anorexia nervosa — clinical features
📷 Image placeholder — Physical signs of anorexia — bradycardia, hypotension, hypothermia, lanugo hair, and the sit-up–squat–stand test (proximal muscle wasting = severity red flag)
Markedly low body weight, intense fear of weight gain, distorted body image, restriction ± excessive exercise/purging.
Physical signs
  • Bradycardia, hypotension, hypothermia, cold peripheries
  • Lanugo hair (fine downy hair — response to loss of body fat)
  • Enlarged salivary glands; amenorrhoea
Red-flag exam sign: the sit-up–squat–stand test — inability to rise without using the arms = severe proximal muscle wasting (a marker of severity/risk).
The biochemical picture
Memory hook: "most things low, but G's and C's raised."
Low High (the G's and C's)
K⁺ (hypokalaemia)Growth hormone
FSH, LH, oestrogen, testosteroneGlucose (cortisol mobilises glucose)
T3Cortisol (stress response)
Cholesterol (cortisol mobilises fat)
Carotinaemia (↑carotene); enlarged salivary glands
Refeeding syndrome is the critical complication — see the Refeeding & Electrolytes tab.
Bulimia nervosa
Recurrent binge eating followed by compensatory purging (self-induced vomiting, laxatives, diuretics, or excessive exercise), driven by over-valuation of weight/shape. Usually normal weight — the key contrast with anorexia.
Signs of purging (high-yield)
  • Russell's sign — calluses/scarring on the knuckles from self-induced vomiting
  • Dental erosion + enamel loss (gastric acid)
  • Enlarged (parotid) salivary glands
  • Hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis (from vomiting)
The vomiting/purging electrolyte picture is covered in the Refeeding & Electrolytes tab (it ties anorexia purging and bulimia together).
ARFID — Avoidant/Restrictive Food Intake Disorder
Restriction or avoidance of food intake leading to nutritional/energy deficiency — weight loss/faltering growth, nutritional deficiency, dependence on supplements, or psychosocial impairment.
The defining feature: the restriction is NOT driven by body-image disturbance or fear of weight gain — this is what separates ARFID from anorexia.
Instead, driven by
  • Sensory sensitivity (texture/taste/smell aversion)
  • Fear of an aversive consequence (e.g. choking, vomiting)
  • Low interest in eating / appetite
More common in children and neurodevelopmental conditions (e.g. autism); a diagnosis of exclusion (rule out anorexia, organic GI causes, other medical illness).
Management: multidisciplinary — dietetic support + psychological therapy (often CBT-based, addressing the specific driver), with family involvement in children.
Refeeding syndrome (critical complication)
📷 Image placeholder — Refeeding pathway — carbohydrate → insulin surge → intracellular shift of phosphate/potassium/magnesium; refeed slowly, replace electrolytes, give thiamine before/with feeding, monitor closely
A dangerous shift when nutrition is reintroduced too quickly in a malnourished patient: carbohydrate → surge in insulin → drives potassium, magnesium and phosphate INTO cells → plasma levels drop. Hallmark = hypophosphataemia, plus fluid shifts and thiamine depletion.
The biochemical triad (high-yield): ↓phosphate, ↓potassium, ↓magnesium.
Features
  • Oedema, confusion, seizures
  • Arrhythmias/tachycardia, cardiac failure
  • Hypokalaemia → ECG changes (prominent U waves, flattened T waves)
Management
  • Identify high-risk patients; refeed slowly
  • Replace phosphate / potassium / magnesium
  • Give thiamine (+ B vitamins) before/with feeding
  • Monitor electrolytes closely; prophylactic supplementation if high-risk
Physiology link: this is the fed-state insulin surge (cross-ref the fed vs fasted metabolism note) applied to a depleted body — insulin drives electrolytes intracellularly faster than depleted stores can tolerate.
The vomiting/purging electrolyte picture
Ties anorexia purging + bulimia together. Recurrent vomiting → hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis:
  • Vomiting loses H⁺ and Cl⁻ → metabolic alkalosis
  • Volume loss → RAAS activation → aldosterone retains Na⁺/water and excretes K⁺ → hypokalaemia
  • Diuretic misuse compounds the potassium loss
  • ECG: hypokalaemia → flattened T waves, U waves
Cross-ref: the RAAS / acid-base physiology — the same picture as any cause of recurrent vomiting.
Assessment (recognition + risk)
  • Clinical diagnosis — history + eating behaviour + body-image beliefs + physical assessment
  • Assess physical risk: weight/BMI trend, obs (bradycardia, hypotension, hypothermia), muscle power (sit-up–squat–stand), bloods (U&E, phosphate, magnesium, glucose, FBC, LFT, TFT), ECG (bradycardia, QTc, hypokalaemia)
  • Screen for comorbid depression, anxiety, OCD, self-harm/suicide risk, substance use
  • SCOFF questionnaire = screening tool; refer to a specialist eating disorder service
Management (NICE NG69)
Overarching principle: psychological therapy is the mainstay; treat medical risk in parallel; drugs have a limited role.
Anorexia nervosa
  • Adults — first-line psychological therapy: individual CBT-ED, MANTRA, or SSCM
  • Children/young people — first-line: anorexia-nervosa-focused family therapy (FT-AN); CBT-ED second-line
  • Manage medical risk alongside (electrolytes, refeeding, monitoring); admit if high physical risk
  • No drug is first-line for anorexia itself
Bulimia nervosa
  • Adults — first-line: bulimia-nervosa-focused guided self-help; if unacceptable/ineffective after ~4 weeks → CBT-ED
  • Children/young people — first-line: family therapy (FT-BN); CBT-ED second-line
  • Drugs: an SSRI (fluoxetine) can reduce binge/purge frequency (adjunct)
Binge eating disorder & ARFID
  • Binge eating disorder: first-line guided self-help → then CBT-ED
  • ARFID: multidisciplinary dietetic + psychological management tailored to the driver
Exam pearls
The three-way split
Anorexia = low weight + body-image disturbance; bulimia = normal weight + binge-purge; ARFID = restricted intake WITHOUT body-image concern.
Anorexia biochemistry
"Most things low, but G's and C's raised" — ↑GH, glucose, cortisol, cholesterol, carotinaemia; ↓K⁺, FSH/LH/oestrogen/testosterone, T3.
Anorexia signs
Bradycardia, hypotension, lanugo hair, enlarged salivary glands; sit-up–squat–stand = severe muscle wasting (red flag).
Bulimia signs
Russell's sign (knuckle calluses), dental erosion, parotid swelling, hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis.
Refeeding syndrome
Insulin surge drives ↓phosphate, ↓potassium, ↓magnesium intracellularly → refeed slowly, replace electrolytes, give thiamine first.
Vomiting picture
Recurrent vomiting → hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis (RAAS-driven K⁺ loss); ECG: flat T, U waves.
Mortality
Anorexia has the highest mortality of any psychiatric disorder.
Anorexia management
Adults → CBT-ED / MANTRA / SSCM; young people → FT-AN (family therapy). No first-line drug.
Bulimia management
Guided self-help → CBT-ED; SSRI (fluoxetine) adjunct.
ARFID management
MDT dietetic + psychological, tailored to the driver.
PSYCHIATRY__Post-Traumatic Stress Disord:
Overview — What & why
A disorder developing after exposure to a traumatic event (actual/threatened death, serious injury or sexual violence — experienced, witnessed, or learned of), characterised by re-experiencing, avoidance, hyperarousal and negative mood/cognition.
The core concept: PTSD is defined by the persistence of a trauma response beyond 1 month — the body stays "stuck" in threat mode long after the danger has passed.
Epidemiology: develops in ~20–30% after significant trauma; often underdiagnosed. Why it matters: the timing-based diagnosis (vs acute stress disorder), the four-cluster framework, therapy-before-drugs, and the strong comorbidity with depression/substance misuse/suicide.
The decisive fork — how long since the trauma?
📷 Image placeholder — Timeline — <4 weeks = acute stress disorder, >1 month (persisting) = PTSD, and a non-catastrophic stressor resolving by ~6 months = adjustment disorder
The same cluster of trauma symptoms is named differently by timing — the key exam discriminator:
Acute stress disorder/reaction PTSD Adjustment disorder
Timingsymptoms in the first 4 weekssymptoms persisting >1 month (≥4 weeks)within ~1 month, resolving within ~6 months
Triggersevere traumasevere trauma (threat to life/integrity)any significant life change (divorce, job loss, illness)
Symptomsintrusion, dissociation, arousal, avoidancethe 4 core clusters (below)low mood/anxiety not meeting full PTSD/depression criteria
The rule (high-yield): <4 weeks = acute stress disorder; >4 weeks = PTSD. Adjustment disorder = a maladaptive response to a non-catastrophic stressor.
The four symptom clusters (core diagnostic framework)
Cluster Features
Re-experiencingflashbacks, nightmares, intrusive distressing images/memories of the event
Avoidanceavoiding people, places, situations or reminders of the trauma
Hyperarousalhypervigilance, exaggerated startle response, irritability, sleep disturbance, poor concentration
Negative mood/cognition (emotional numbing)detachment, inability to feel emotions, negative beliefs, guilt/shame
Diagnosis: symptoms from these clusters present for ≥1 month and causing significant distress/impairment. Memory hook: reliving · avoiding · on-edge · numb.
Risk factors & associations
Risk factors
  • Trauma type: interpersonal/deliberate (assault, combat, sexual violence) > accidental; repeated/prolonged trauma
  • Personal: previous mental illness, lack of social support, prior trauma, female sex
Associations (high-yield)
  • Strongly associated with depression, substance misuse and suicide risk — always screen
  • Complex PTSD: from prolonged/repeated trauma (childhood abuse, captivity) — adds affect dysregulation, negative self-concept and relationship difficulties
Assessment (largely clinical)
  • Clinical diagnosis — careful trauma history (ask directly; patients often avoid disclosing) + symptom clusters + ≥1 month duration
  • Screen for comorbid depression, substance misuse and suicide/self-harm risk
  • Rule out other diagnoses (depression, adjustment disorder, other anxiety disorders, psychosis if dissociative flashbacks are prominent)
  • No diagnostic test; validated trauma screening questionnaires can aid
Management (NICE NG116 — therapy is first-line)
📷 Image placeholder — Decision flow — trauma-focused CBT or EMDR first-line for all; venlafaxine or an SSRI only if the patient prefers/declines/cannot access therapy or has comorbid depression; benzodiazepines excluded
Overarching principle: trauma-focused psychological therapy is first-line — NOT drugs.
Early (within the first month)
  • Mild symptoms <4 weeks → watchful waiting, with follow-up within 1 month
  • Severe symptoms in the first month → trauma-focused CBT (don't wait)
Established PTSD (>1 month) — psychological therapy first-line
  • Trauma-focused CBT (TF-CBT) — first-line (typically 8–12 sessions)
  • OR EMDR (Eye Movement Desensitisation & Reprocessing) — equally recommended first-line
  • EMDR is NOT recommended for combat-related trauma
  • Offered before drug treatment
Drug treatment (second-line / adjunct)
  • Used if the person prefers medication, declines/can't access therapy, or has comorbid depression
  • First-line drugs: venlafaxine or an SSRI (sertraline and paroxetine are UK-licensed for PTSD; venlafaxine and fluoxetine are used off-label)
  • Severe/refractory or psychotic symptoms: add an antipsychotic (risperidone/quetiapine) as augmentation
  • Prazosin can help trauma-related nightmares
Important correction (high-yield): do NOT use benzodiazepines for PTSD — current NICE advises against them (they don't treat PTSD, worsen outcomes, and risk dependence). Older notes suggesting BZDs for acute symptoms reflect outdated practice.
Exam pearls
Timing defines it
PTSD = trauma response persisting >1 month (≥4 weeks); acute stress disorder = <4 weeks.
Adjustment disorder
Response to a non-catastrophic stressor (divorce, job loss), not a life-threat.
Four clusters
Re-experiencing (flashbacks/nightmares), avoidance, hyperarousal (hypervigilance/startle), negative mood/emotional numbing.
First-line = therapy
Trauma-focused CBT or EMDR — NOT drugs.
EMDR caveat
Not recommended for combat-related trauma.
Mild + <4 weeks
Watchful waiting; follow up within 1 month.
Drugs are 2nd-line
Venlafaxine or SSRI (sertraline); augment with an antipsychotic (risperidone) if severe; prazosin for nightmares.
Avoid benzodiazepines
Current NICE — dependence, poor outcomes.
Always screen
Comorbid depression, substance misuse and suicide risk.
Complex PTSD
Prolonged/repeated trauma + affect dysregulation + negative self-concept.
PSYCHIATRY__Bipolar Affective Disorder:
Overview — What & why
A chronic mood disorder defined by episodes of mania/hypomania alternating with depression, with periods of normal (euthymic) mood between.
The core concept: bipolar is separated from unipolar depression by the presence of at least one manic or hypomanic episode — so the single most important clinical question is "has there ever been a high?"
Epidemiology: onset typically late teens–20s; strong genetic component; high suicide risk (~15×). Why it matters: underpins mood-stabiliser pharmacology (lithium/valproate), the danger of unopposed antidepressants, and the mania/hypomania and type I/II distinctions.
The decisive fork — mania vs hypomania (defines the type)
📷 Image placeholder — Criteria table — mania (≥7 days, severe impairment ± psychosis, may need admission) vs hypomania (≥4 days, function preserved, no psychosis); psychosis or marked impairment = mania
Both are abnormally elevated or irritable mood with ↑energy, ↓need for sleep, pressured speech, grandiosity, distractibility and disinhibition/risk-taking — the difference is severity, duration and psychosis:
Mania Hypomania
Duration≥7 days<7 days (≥4 days)
Functional impairmentsevere — disrupts work/social functionmild — some change, function largely preserved
Hospitalisationmay be needed (risk to self/others)unlikely
Psychotic symptomscan occur (grandiose delusions, hallucinations)never (no psychosis)
The rule (high-yield): psychosis OR marked impairment/hospitalisation = mania; milder, no psychosis, function preserved = hypomania. Psychotic features automatically make it mania.
The two types
Bipolar I Bipolar II
Defining episodemania (± depression)hypomania + depression (never full mania)
Notemania alone diagnoses it (depression not required)requires both hypomania and depressive episodes
The distinction: Bipolar I = mania; Bipolar II = hypomania + depression. If they have ever had a true manic episode → it's type I.
Cyclothymia = milder chronic mood fluctuation (subthreshold highs and lows) not meeting full criteria for bipolar.
Recognising a manic episode
Mood & cognition
  • Mood: elevated/euphoric or irritable
  • Flight of ideas (rapid speech, leaping between topics with discernible links)
  • Grandiosity / grandiose delusions
  • Distractibility, poor insight
Behaviour
  • ↓need for sleep, ↑goal-directed activity
  • Disinhibition; pressured/rapid speech
  • Reckless behaviour — overspending, risky sex, impulsive decisions
  • Severe: psychosis (grandiose/persecutory delusions, hallucinations)
High-yield speech sign: flight of ideas (leaps with links) is the manic thought disorder — contrast with knight's move (no links) in schizophrenia.
Investigations
Exclude secondary causes
  • Bloods: TFT (hyperthyroidism), U&E, LFT, glucose, calcium
  • Urine drug screen (stimulants)
  • Imaging if atypical / focal signs
  • Exclude steroid-induced mania, substance use
Baseline before mood stabilisers (high-yield)
  • Lithium: U&E + eGFR, TFT, calcium (affects kidney/thyroid/parathyroid)
  • Valproate: LFT + FBC
  • Antipsychotics: weight/BMI, glucose, lipids, ECG
  • Pregnancy test / contraception (valproate + lithium teratogenic)
Diagnosis is clinical — a collateral history is invaluable (patients often lack insight into highs).
Management (NICE — acute vs long-term)
Overarching principle: treat the acute episode → maintain long-term prophylaxis → watch antidepressants (they can trigger mania).
Acute mania / hypomania
  • Not on treatment → antipsychotic (olanzapine, quetiapine, risperidone, or haloperidol) — first-line
  • Already on treatment → optimise / add
  • STOP any antidepressant (it may be driving the mania)
  • Agitation: with agitation → IM antipsychotic ± benzodiazepine; without → oral antipsychotic monotherapy
Acute bipolar depression
  • Do NOT use an antidepressant alone (risk of switching to mania)
  • Options: quetiapine, olanzapine (± fluoxetine), or lamotrigine; + CBT
  • Never unopposed antidepressant monotherapy — highest switch risk with venlafaxine / TCAs
Long-term prophylaxis: LITHIUM = first-line mood stabiliser (most effective; also ↓ suicide risk). If ineffective/not tolerated → valproate (2nd-line) or an antipsychotic (e.g. quetiapine), ± combine.
CRITICAL valproate restriction (current): do NOT start valproate in anyone (male or female) under 55 unless two specialists independently document there is no alternative — due to teratogenicity and fertility/testicular effects. Never in women of childbearing potential without a pregnancy prevention programme.
Psychosocial: psychoeducation, CBT, mood monitoring, sleep/routine regulation, address substance use. CMHT referral — routine if hypomania; urgent if mania or severe depression.
Lithium — the drug reference (high-yield)
📷 Image placeholder — Lithium therapeutic vs toxic — fine tremor (therapeutic) vs coarse tremor, ataxia, dysarthria, confusion, seizures (toxic); precipitants (dehydration, NSAIDs, ACEi/ARB, thiazides) → stop lithium, IV fluids, ± dialysis
Use: bipolar prophylaxis (1st-line), refractory depression augmentation; ↓ suicide risk. Mechanism: interferes with cAMP + inositol triphosphate second-messenger signalling. Narrow therapeutic index → needs monitoring.
Side effects — mnemonic LITHIUM
  • Lethargy · Insipidus (nephrogenic diabetes insipidus → polyuria) · Tremor (fine)
  • Hypothyroidism · Insides (GI: nausea, diarrhoea) · Urine ↑ · Metallic taste
  • Plus: weight gain, nephrotoxicity, hyperparathyroidism → hypercalcaemia, benign leucocytosis, T-wave flattening/inversion
Lithium toxicity: precipitated by dehydration, illness, renal impairment, and drug interactions (NSAIDs, ACEi/ARB, thiazides) — all ↓ lithium clearance.
Features: coarse tremor (vs fine tremor at therapeutic level), ataxia, dysarthria, confusion, nystagmus, seizures, arrhythmias, visual disturbance — often GI first (vomiting/diarrhoea) then neurological.
Management: stop lithium, IV fluids (rehydrate → ↑ excretion), correct electrolytes, seizure control, haemodialysis if severe.
Monitoring
  • Levels taken 12 hours post-dose
  • Weekly after starting / dose change until stable, then every 3 months
  • TFT + renal function (U&E/eGFR) every 6 months; calcium
Valproate — the drug reference (high-yield)
Use: bipolar (2nd-line prophylaxis, acute mania) — but see the <55 restriction above. Mechanism: blocks voltage-gated Na⁺ channels; CYP enzyme inhibitor.
Side effects — mnemonic VALPROATE
  • Vomiting · Alopecia · Liver toxicity · Pancreatitis / Pancytopenia
  • Retention of fat (weight gain) · Oedema · Anorexia · Tremor · Enzyme inhibition
TERATOGENIC (neural tube defects, neurodevelopmental effects) → avoid in pregnancy / women of childbearing potential. This is the reason for the strict prescribing restriction.
Antipsychotics in bipolar
Used for acute mania, bipolar depression (quetiapine, olanzapine) and prophylaxis. Same side-effect profile as in schizophrenia — EPSEs, metabolic effects, hyperprolactinaemia, NMS. Cross-ref the Schizophrenia / Psychosis note for the full antipsychotic reference.
Exam pearls
Defining feature
Bipolar = ≥1 manic OR hypomanic episode — the "high" separates it from unipolar depression.
Mania vs hypomania
Mania ≥7 days, severe impairment, ± psychosis; hypomania <7 days, function preserved, NO psychosis. Psychosis = mania.
Types
Bipolar I = mania; Bipolar II = hypomania + depression.
Speech sign
Flight of ideas (leaps with links) = mania; knight's move (no links) = schizophrenia.
Acute mania
Antipsychotic + STOP antidepressant; agitation → IM antipsychotic ± benzodiazepine.
Bipolar depression
NEVER antidepressant monotherapy (switch risk, worst with venlafaxine); quetiapine/olanzapine ± fluoxetine/lamotrigine + mood stabiliser.
Prophylaxis
LITHIUM first-line (also ↓ suicide).
Lithium monitoring
Levels 12h post-dose; every 3 months; TFT/renal every 6 months. Narrow therapeutic index.
Lithium toxicity
Precipitated by dehydration/NSAIDs/ACEi/thiazides → coarse tremor, ataxia, confusion → IV fluids.
Valproate
Teratogenic; don't start in under-55s without 2 specialists agreeing; VALPROATE side effects.
Antidepressant caution
Can trigger mania — highest risk with venlafaxine.
PSYCHIATRY__Schizophrenia / Psychosis:
Overview — Psychosis vs Schizophrenia
Psychosis = loss of contact with reality, defined by positive symptoms: delusions (fixed false beliefs), hallucinations (perceptions without a stimulus) and thought disorder (disorganised speech/thinking). Psychosis is the symptom.
Schizophrenia = a chronic psychotic disorder with positive + negative symptoms + functional decline, lasting ≥1 month of active symptoms (DSM-5 also requires ≥6 months total continuous disturbance). Schizophrenia is one cause of psychosis.
The organising principle: psychosis is a syndrome with many causes — the whole diagnostic job is (1) exclude organic & drug causes, then (2) characterise the primary psychiatric disorder using the positive/negative framework and duration.
Epidemiology: ~1% lifetime risk; peak onset late teens–20s in men, 20s–30s in women; strong genetic component (highest risk with an affected identical twin). Why it matters: underpins the MSE, the first-rank symptoms, antipsychotic pharmacology, and the psychiatric emergencies (NMS). Patients die ~15–20 years early, mostly from cardiovascular disease.
The decisive fork — primary (psychiatric) vs secondary (organic/drug)
The first and most important split. Always exclude organic + drug causes before diagnosing a primary psychotic disorder.
Primary psychiatric Secondary (organic / drug-induced)
Causesschizophrenia, schizoaffective, bipolar/mania, psychotic depression, brief psychotic disorderDrugs: stimulants, cannabis, steroids, dopaminergics, withdrawal states. Organic: delirium, dementia, temporal lobe epilepsy, encephalitis (incl. autoimmune/anti-NMDA), SLE, brain tumour, B12 deficiency
Clues to secondary—acute onset, older age, clouded/fluctuating consciousness, VISUAL hallucinations, focal neurology, abnormal obs/bloods
Consciousnessclear sensoriumoften impaired (esp. delirium)
Rule of thumb (high-yield): visual hallucinations + clouded consciousness → think organic/delirium, not schizophrenia. Schizophrenic hallucinations are characteristically auditory with a clear sensorium.
The symptom framework — positive vs negative (the core)
Positive symptoms (added experiences) Negative symptoms (lost function)
Delusions (esp. persecutory, delusions of control)Blunted / incongruous affect
Hallucinations (esp. auditory — 3rd-person, running commentary, thought echo)Anhedonia (no pleasure)
Thought disorder (disorganised speech)Alogia (poverty of speech)
Passivity phenomena (actions/feelings externally controlled)Avolition (poor motivation) + social withdrawal
Positive symptoms respond well to antipsychotics; negative symptoms are harder to treat and drive long-term disability. Negative symptoms + a preceding prodrome of social withdrawal point to schizophrenia over a brief/drug-induced psychosis. Remember the 4 A's of negative symptoms: Affect (blunted), Anhedonia, Alogia, Avolition.
Schneider's first-rank symptoms (classic exam framework)
Historically associated with schizophrenia — not diagnostic alone, but a classic exam framework.
First-rank symptom Example
Auditory hallucinations2+ voices discussing the patient in the 3rd person, thought echo, running commentary on behaviour
Thought alienationthought insertion, withdrawal, broadcasting
Passivity phenomenabodily sensations / actions / impulses felt to be externally controlled
Delusional perceptiona normal perception given sudden bizarre delusional meaning ("the traffic light turned green, therefore I am the King")
Other schizophrenia features from your notes: catatonia (immobility / bizarre posturing), neologisms, and impaired insight.
Thought disorder & delusion terminology (exam favourite)
Formal thought disorder (disorganised speech):
Term Meaning
Circumstantialityexcessive detail but eventually answers
Tangentialitywanders off and never returns
Knight's move thinkingillogical leaps between unrelated ideas (no discernible link)
Flight of ideasrapid leaps with discernible links (a manic feature)
Neologismsmade-up words

Perseverationrepeating ideas/words despite topic change
Echolaliarepeating others' speech
High-yield discriminator: knight's move = NO logical link (schizophrenia) vs flight of ideas = links present (mania).
Delusion types
  • Persecutory — being conspired against (classic paranoid schizophrenia)
  • Grandiose — special powers/identity (mania)
  • Nihilistic — dead / world ended (psychotic depression, Cotard's)
  • Delusions of control / passivity — thoughts or actions controlled by an external force
  • Somatic — a physical/medical problem despite no evidence
Investigations
Purpose 1 — exclude organic / drug cause
  • Bloods: FBC, U&E, LFT, TFT, glucose, calcium, B12/folate
  • Urine drug screen
  • CT/MRI head if new-onset, focal signs, atypical features
  • Autoimmune encephalitis screen (anti-NMDA) if rapid onset + neuro/autonomic features
  • HIV / syphilis serology if indicated
Purpose 2 — baseline before antipsychotics (high-yield)
  • Weight/BMI, waist circumference
  • Blood glucose / HbA1c, lipids
  • Prolactin
  • ECG (QTc), U&E, LFT
  • Why: antipsychotics cause metabolic + QTc + prolactin effects
Diagnosis is clinical (DSM-5: active symptoms ≥1 month + ≥6 months total continuous disturbance; ICD-11: ≥1 month) for schizophrenia. There is no diagnostic test.
Management (NICE — biopsychosocial)
Acute / first-episode — first-line
  • Oral atypical (2nd-gen) antipsychotic — e.g. risperidone, olanzapine, aripiprazole, quetiapine (choice guided by side-effect profile)
  • PLUS CBT (NICE: offer to all, ≥16 sessions) + family intervention
  • Refer to an Early Intervention in Psychosis (EIP) service for a first episode
Antipsychotic principles
  • Trial one antipsychotic at an adequate dose for 4–6 weeks before switching
  • If inadequate → switch to a second, different antipsychotic
  • Poor adherence → long-acting IM depot injection
  • Monitor metabolic / prolactin / QTc effects
Treatment-resistant schizophrenia (high-yield): inadequate response to ≥2 adequate antipsychotic trials (at least one an atypical) → CLOZAPINE — the most effective antipsychotic for TRS, reserved because of agranulocytosis risk.
Also: psychoeducation, social support / supported employment, treat comorbid depression & substance misuse, and active CVD risk management (leading cause of premature death).
Antipsychotics — the drug reference (high-yield)
📷 Image placeholder — EPSE onset timeline — acute dystonia (hours–days, procyclidine) → akathisia & parkinsonism (days–weeks) → tardive dyskinesia (months–years, often irreversible)
📷 Image placeholder — The four dopamine pathways — mesolimbic (blockade → ↓positive symptoms, therapeutic), mesocortical (worsens negative symptoms), nigrostriatal (EPSEs) and tuberoinfundibular (↑prolactin)
Mechanism: mainly dopamine D2 antagonism — blocking the mesolimbic pathway ↓ positive symptoms, but off-target D2 blockade causes side effects (nigrostriatal → EPSEs; tuberoinfundibular → ↑ prolactin).
Typical (1st-gen) Atypical (2nd-gen)
Exampleshaloperidol, chlorpromazinerisperidone, olanzapine, quetiapine, aripiprazole, clozapine
Main mechanismstrong D2 antagonismD2 + 5-HT2 antagonism
Key side effectsextrapyramidal (EPSEs) + hyperprolactinaemiametabolic (weight gain, diabetes, dyslipidaemia)
Extrapyramidal side effects (EPSEs) — classic typical-antipsychotic toxicity:
EPSE Feature Onset Treatment
Acute dystoniasustained contraction (torticollis, oculogyric crisis)hours–daysprocyclidine (anticholinergic)
Akathisiasevere inner restlessnessdays–weeksreduce dose / propranolol
Parkinsonismbradykinesia, rigidity, tremorweeksreduce dose / anticholinergic

Key drug-specific points
  • Aripiprazole — fewest side effects, least prolactin rise ("ariPPrazole is aPPropriate" when prolactin is a concern)
  • Haloperidol — QTc prolongation
  • Olanzapine / clozapine — most weight gain / metabolic effect
  • Clozapine (TRS only) — agranulocytosis/neutropenia (mandatory FBC monitoring), myocarditis (baseline ECG), reduced seizure threshold, constipation (can be fatal — ileus), hypersalivation; missed >48h → re-titrate from low dose; smoking cessation ↑ clozapine levels
  • All antipsychotics — ↑ stroke + VTE risk; hyperprolactinaemia (galactorrhoea, ↓ libido, menstrual disturbance); risk of NMS
Neuroleptic malignant syndrome — the emergency
A life-threatening reaction to dopamine blockade: fever, muscle rigidity ("lead-pipe"), autonomic instability (↑HR, ↑BP, sweating), confusion. Bloods: ↑↑ CK (rhabdomyolysis → AKI), ↑ WCC.
Management
  • STOP the antipsychotic
  • Supportive care, IV fluids, active cooling
  • Dantrolene ± bromocriptine in severe cases
vs serotonin syndrome: NMS = rigidity + hyporeflexia, onset over days; serotonin syndrome = hyperreflexia/clonus + agitation, rapid onset.
Prognosis
Poor prognostic factors Better prognosis
strong family historyacute onset
gradual (insidious) onsetobvious precipitant
low IQ; prodrome of social withdrawalprominent positive (not negative) symptoms
prominent negative symptoms; no clear precipitant; male sex; early onsetgood premorbid functioning
Exam pearls
Exclude organic first
Visual hallucinations + clouded consciousness → organic/delirium, not schizophrenia (schizophrenia = auditory, clear sensorium).
Duration
Schizophrenia = ≥6 months; brief psychotic disorder <1 month (resolves to baseline).
Positive vs negative
Positive symptoms respond to antipsychotics; negative symptoms don't — and drive disability.
Schneider's first-rank
3rd-person auditory hallucinations, thought insertion/withdrawal/broadcasting, passivity, delusional perception.
Speech discriminator
Knight's move = no link (schizophrenia) vs flight of ideas = links present (mania).
First-line
Oral atypical antipsychotic + CBT + family intervention.
Treatment-resistant
≥2 failed antipsychotic trials → CLOZAPINE.
Clozapine
Agranulocytosis (FBC monitoring), myocarditis (baseline ECG), missed >48h → re-titrate, smoking cessation ↑ levels.
EPSEs
Acute dystonia (procyclidine), tardive dyskinesia (late, tetrabenazine), akathisia, parkinsonism — typical > atypical.
Drug specifics
Aripiprazole (a D2 partial agonist) = fewest SEs + least prolactin; haloperidol = QTc.
NMS
Fever + rigidity + autonomic instability + ↑↑CK → stop drug, dantrolene.
Poor prognosis
Insidious onset, negative symptoms, social-withdrawal prodrome, low IQ, strong FHx.
PSYCHIATRY__Delusional & Misidentificati:
Overview — What & why
A group of disorders defined by specific, characteristic delusions — fixed false beliefs held despite contradictory evidence — several with classic eponymous names (Capgras, Cotard, Othello…).
The core concept: organise these by what the delusion is about — misidentification (people/identity), content themes (jealousy, love, death, infestation), or isolated delusional disorder. Each can be a primary delusion or secondary to another condition (psychosis, mood disorder, dementia, organic disease) — so always identify the delusion type AND find its cause.
The eponyms are exam favourites; the higher-yield skill is recognising the pattern + the conditions each is associated with.
The decisive fork — primary or secondary?
Primary Secondary
Causeprimary psychotic/delusional disorderorganic (dementia — esp. Lewy body, delirium, brain lesion, epilepsy) or another psychiatric disorder (schizophrenia, mood disorder with psychosis)
Clue to secondary—older age, cognitive impairment, acute onset, fluctuation, focal signs, a mood episode
The rule (high-yield): the misidentification syndromes (Capgras, Fregoli) are frequently secondary to organic disease (dementia, especially Lewy body dementia) as well as schizophrenia → always consider an organic cause, particularly in older patients. Cotard's is classically secondary to severe (psychotic) depression; Othello's and erotomania can be primary or secondary.
Delusion terminology (the descriptive vocabulary)
The general delusion types by content (these underlie the named syndromes):
Delusion Content Classic association
Persecutorybeing conspired against/harmedparanoid schizophrenia

Nihilisticself/body/world dead or non-existentpsychotic depression (→ Cotard's)

Syndrome The delusion Memory hook

Capgras vs Fregoli (high-yield): Capgras = familiar person seen as a stranger/impostor ("you're not really my husband"); Fregoli = strangers seen as a familiar person in disguise ("that stranger is really my husband in disguise") — mirror images. Both are frequently associated with organic disease (dementia, neurological lesions) as well as schizophrenia → investigate for an organic cause.
The thematic delusional syndromes (delusions by content)
Syndrome The delusion Associations / key points

Othello risk point (high-yield): pathological jealousy carries a significant risk of violence/harm to the partner → a forensic-risk delusion that must be taken seriously.
Charles-Bonnet syndrome (a hallucination, NOT a delusion)
Charles-Bonnet syndrome = complex visual hallucinations in people with significant visual impairment/eye disease (macular degeneration, glaucoma), in clear consciousness and with insight. Hallucinations are typically faces, children and animals; the person usually knows they aren't real.
Key distinction (high-yield): this is a release phenomenon of visual loss — NOT a psychosis or delusion (insight retained, no other psychotic features) → do not misdiagnose as a psychotic disorder. Management = reassurance + optimising vision / treating the eye disease. (Grouped with these eponyms, but conceptually a perceptual disorder, not a delusion.)
Assessment (identify the delusion + find the cause)
  • Clinical diagnosis — characterise the delusion (content, conviction, fixity), assess insight, full mental state exam
  • Always look for an underlying cause: psychiatric (schizophrenia, psychotic depression → Cotard's, mania, delusional disorder); organic (dementia esp. Lewy body, delirium, brain lesion, epilepsy, substance misuse) — especially with misidentification syndromes and in older patients → consider cognitive assessment + neuroimaging
  • Assess risk: particularly Othello syndrome (violence to partner) and erotomania (stalking/harassment)
Management (treat the delusion + the underlying cause)
Overarching principle: treat the underlying condition; antipsychotics for the delusion; address risk.
  • Treat the underlying cause: antidepressants (± antipsychotics/ECT) for Cotard's (psychotic depression); antipsychotics for schizophrenia-related delusions; treat the organic cause if identified (caution re antipsychotics in Lewy body dementia — cross-ref)
  • Antipsychotics for the delusional content (delusional disorder, primary psychosis)
  • Charles-Bonnet: reassurance + optimise vision (not antipsychotics)
  • Risk management: Othello syndrome — assess/manage risk to the partner (may need separation/safeguarding); erotomania — manage stalking risk
  • Delusional parasitosis: treat underlying cause; antipsychotics; dermatology + psychiatry liaison
Exam pearls
Primary or secondary?
Misidentification syndromes (Capgras/Fregoli) are often organic (dementia, esp. Lewy body); Cotard's → severe/psychotic depression.

Fregoli
Strangers are a familiar person in disguise (the mirror image of Capgras).
Cotard's
Belief that one is dead/non-existent (nihilistic; psychotic depression).
Othello syndrome
Pathological jealousy (partner unfaithful) → high violence risk to partner.
De Clérambault (erotomania)
Belief someone (higher status) is secretly in love with them → stalking risk.
Delusional parasitosis (Ekbom)
Belief of being infested → excoriations, matchbox sign.

Complex visual hallucinations with EYE DISEASE, clear consciousness + INSIGHT — NOT a psychosis → reassurance + treat vision.
Management
Treat the underlying cause + antipsychotic for the delusion; assess risk (Othello, erotomania).
PSYCHIATRY__Psychotropic Drug Classes:
Overview — What & why
A consolidated reference for the major psychotropic drug classes — antipsychotics, antidepressants, mood stabilisers, anxiolytics/hypnotics, and stimulants — pulling together the drug detail spread across the condition notes.
The core concept: most psychotropics act on monoamine or GABA neurotransmission, and their side effects are largely predictable from their receptor actions. Getting the class → mechanism → key side effects → monitoring grid right lets you reason out most of psychopharmacology.
The five cross-class emergencies to recognise: NMS, serotonin syndrome, lithium toxicity, clozapine agranulocytosis, and the tyramine (MAOI) crisis — see the Emergencies tab.

Lithium (1st-line bipolar prophylaxis)
Mechanism: interferes with cAMP + inositol triphosphate. Narrow therapeutic index.
  • Side effects (LITHIUM): Lethargy, Insipidus (nephrogenic DI), Tremor (fine), Hypothyroidism, Insides (GI), Urine ↑, Metallic taste; + weight gain, nephrotoxicity, hyperparathyroidism → hypercalcaemia, benign leucocytosis, T-wave changes
  • Toxicity: precipitated by dehydration, NSAIDs, ACEi/ARB, thiazides; coarse tremor, ataxia, dysarthria, confusion, seizures, arrhythmias (often GI first, then neuro) → stop, IV fluids, ± dialysis
  • Monitoring (high-yield): levels 12h post-dose; weekly until stable → 3-monthly; TFT + renal 6-monthly
Other mood stabilisers
Valproate: VALPROATE side effects; teratogenic; do NOT start in under-55s without 2 specialists documenting there's no alternative; avoid in women of childbearing potential.
  • Lamotrigine: bipolar depression; watch for Stevens-Johnson syndrome → slow titration
  • Antipsychotics (quetiapine, olanzapine) are also used as mood stabilisers

Exam pearls
Antipsychotics
D2 antagonism; typical → EPSEs + prolactin, atypical → metabolic; acute dystonia → procyclidine, tardive dyskinesia → tetrabenazine; aripiprazole = least prolactin; clozapine → agranulocytosis (FBC) + myocarditis (ECG); NMS = rigidity + ↑CK → dantrolene.
Antidepressants
SSRI 1st-line (sertraline) — GI bleed/hyponatraemia/citalopram-QT; SNRI → check BP; mirtazapine → sedation + appetite; TCA → dangerous overdose; MAOI → tyramine crisis; serotonin syndrome = clonus + hyperreflexia → cyproheptadine.
Mood stabilisers
Lithium 1st-line bipolar prophylaxis; levels 12h post-dose, 3-monthly + TFT/renal 6-monthly; toxicity from dehydration/NSAIDs/thiazides; valproate teratogenic (under-55 restriction); lamotrigine → SJS.
Anxiolytics/hypnotics
Benzodiazepines/Z-drugs = short-term only (dependence); enhance GABA; not for chronic GAD/PTSD/insomnia; chlordiazepoxide for alcohol withdrawal (lorazepam if liver failure).
Stimulants
Methylphenidate (ADHD) — monitor growth + CVS.
The 5 emergencies
NMS, serotonin syndrome, lithium toxicity, clozapine agranulocytosis, tyramine crisis.
